title: Memory leak: transient models using Enum methods or Field(exclude_if=...) survive GC
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Transient `BaseModel` classes are not collected when either:
* A model field references an `Enum` whose class defines a Python method.
* A model field uses `Field(exclude_if=<Python callable>)`.

After the defining module is removed from `sys.modules` and every ordinary strong reference is dropped, weak references to the model and enum classes remain alive after repeated full `gc.collect()` calls. Repeating this construction in disposable module namespaces causes linear memory growth.

Controls using an enum without methods or a field without `exclude_if` are collected normally.

I encountered this in combination with a Temporal workflow sandbox. With a large interconnected model graph and high volume Temporal workflows this can result in multi-GiB process growth relatively quickly.

The likely cause is missing `PyGcTraverse` edges for Python objects held by pydantic-core:
* `SerField` owns `serialization_exclude_if`, but traverses only `serializer`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/serializers/fields.rs#L26-L38
* `EnumSerializer` owns `class`, but traverses only `serializer`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/serializers/type_serializers/enum_.rs
* Each `EnumValidator<T>` owns `lookup`, but traverses only `class` and `missing`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/validators/enum_.rs

Traversing `py_schema` does not compensate for another unreported direct reference: CPython’s collector accounts for every actual strong edge individually.

I tested a temporary build from Pydantic `main` at `c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c`. Adding only these traversal edges made all objects in the reproduction collectible:
* Add `serialization_exclude_if` to `SerField` traversal.
* Add `class` to `EnumSerializer` traversal.
* Add `lookup` to every `EnumValidator<T>` traversal.

For the enum case, changing only the serializer or only the validator was insufficient; both missing edges were required.

This appears related to earlier missing-traversal fixes such as:

* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/5136
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/787
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1100

I would be happy to submit a focused patch.

(please note that this analysis was LLM assisted)

### Example Code

```Python
import gc
import sys
import types
import weakref

def transient_module(name, source, class_names):
    module = types.ModuleType(name)
    sys.modules[name] = module
    exec(compile(source, f"<{name}>", "exec"), module.__dict__)
    refs = tuple(
        weakref.ref(module.__dict__[class_name])
        for class_name in class_names
    )
    del sys.modules[name]
    del module
    return refs

enum_ref, enum_model_ref = transient_module(
    "_pydantic_enum_gc_repro",
    """
from enum import Enum
from pydantic import BaseModel
class Membership(str, Enum):
    FULL = "full"
    def label(self) -> str:
        return self.value
class Model(BaseModel):
    membership: Membership
""",
    ("Membership", "Model"),
)

(exclude_if_model_ref,) = transient_module(
    "_pydantic_exclude_if_gc_repro",
    """
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
class Model(BaseModel):
    value: int = Field(exclude_if=lambda value: False)
""",
    ("Model",),
)

for _ in range(5):
    gc.collect()

# All three should be False because no intentional strong references remain.
print("enum alive:", enum_ref() is not None)
print("enum model alive:", enum_model_ref() is not None)
print("exclude_if model alive:", exclude_if_model_ref() is not None)
```

title: Generic model parametrization drops field defaults and typevar substitution after `__annotations__` is read on a metaclass (Python <= 3.13)
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

This is a regression on `main` (`2.14.0a1`); I could not reproduce it on any released version (checked 2.13.4 and 2.10.6 under the same conditions). It affects Python 3.10–3.13 (verified on 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13); Python 3.14 is unaffected.

If `__annotations__` has ever been **read** on a metaclass appearing in a model's metatype MRO (e.g. `ModelMetaclass` itself, or `abc.ABCMeta`), then any generic model parametrized **for the first time afterwards** gets a broken schema:

- type variables are not substituted (`x: T` ends up with an `any` schema), and
- field defaults are dropped (fields with defaults become required).

Parametrizations built *before* the read keep working, since their schemas are already cached — which makes this very order-dependent and confusing to track down in a real test suite.

Reading an attribute sounds like an odd trigger, but it happens in the wild: on CPython ≤ 3.13, reading `__annotations__` on a (heap) class that has none **auto-creates a plain `__annotations__ = {}` entry in that class's `__dict__`** (see the [annotations HOWTO](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/annotations.html)). `langgraph` does such a read at import time (`get_cached_annotated_keys` in `langgraph/_internal/_fields.py` has a `getattr(base, "__annotations__", None)` fallback — added for Python 3.14 compat, ironically — which ends up planting `{}` on `abc.ABCMeta`). So a plain `import langgraph.prebuilt` breaks all subsequently-parametrized generic models. We found this via the `pydantic/logfire` weekly CI job testing against pydantic main, where `pydantic_evals.Dataset.from_dict()` fails with `3 validation errors for _DatasetModel[...]` — `Field required` for exactly its three defaulted fields — but only in test runs where a langchain test ran first ([failing run](https://github.com/pydantic/logfire/actions/runs/30268424934)).

**Mechanism:**

1. The planted `{}` lives in the metaclass's `__dict__`. For a model class `M`, attribute lookup of `M.__annotations__` searches `type(M).__mro__` (e.g. `(ModelMetaclass, ABCMeta, type, object)`) and now finds the plain dict **before** reaching the `type.__annotations__` getset descriptor. A plain dict is not a data descriptor, so lookup falls back to `M`'s own MRO — and for a class with no own `__annotations__` (like a freshly created generic submodel), this returns **the parent's annotations**. (Normally the `type.__annotations__` data descriptor intercepts the lookup and auto-creates/returns the class's own empty dict, which is what makes `getattr` look safe.)
2. `safe_get_annotations()` in `pydantic/_internal/_typing_extra.py` uses `getattr(obj, '__annotations__', {})` on < 3.14, so for the new submodel `G[str]` it returns the origin's annotations instead of `{}`:
   ```
   clean:    safe_get_annotations(G[str]) == {}
   poisoned: safe_get_annotations(G[str]) == {'x': ~T, 'a': <class 'int'>}
   ```
3. In `collect_model_fields()`, `cls_annotations` is "only used to determine if an annotation comes from a parent class". The leak makes `ann_name in cls_annotations` true for every inherited field, so instead of copying the parent `FieldInfo` and applying `typevars_map` (via `_recreate_field_info`), it takes the plain `FieldInfo.from_annotation(ann_type)` branch: no typevar substitution, and no default — the origin's class-attribute default is long gone because it was `delattr`'d during the origin's own field collection.

**Possible fix:** for classes on ≤ 3.13, read own annotations via `obj.__dict__.get('__annotations__', {})` (what `inspect.get_annotations()` does) rather than `getattr`. Both call sites of `safe_get_annotations()` seem to want own-class annotations anyway: `get_model_type_hints()` iterates the MRO itself and calls it per base, and `cls_annotations` in `collect_model_fields()` is explicitly meant to be the current class's own annotations.

title: Experimental pipeline: every constraint chained after `ge`/`lt`/`le` is dropped from the JSON schema
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

In the experimental pipeline API, chaining constraints silently drops every bound after the first from the generated JSON schema. **Validation stays correct** - only the published schema is wrong, which makes it easy to miss.

All bounds below are non-zero, so this is not #13450 (falsy zero bounds in `Interval`). Observed identically on released 2.13.4 and on `main` (2.14.0a1).

| expression | JSON schema | validation |
|---|---|---|
| `validate_as(int).ge(1).le(100)` | `{"minimum": 1, "type": "integer"}` | 0 reject, 50 accept, 200 reject |
| `validate_as(int).le(100).ge(1)` | `{"maximum": 100, "type": "integer"}` | 0 reject, 50 accept, 200 reject |
| `validate_as(int).constrain(Interval(ge=1, le=100))` | `{"minimum": 1, "type": "integer"}` | 0 reject, 50 accept, 200 reject |
| `validate_as(int).ge(1).le(100).multiple_of(5)` | `{"minimum": 1, "type": "integer"}` | correct |
| `validate_as(int).gt(1).lt(100)` *(control)* | `{"exclusiveMinimum": 1, "exclusiveMaximum": 100, ...}` | correct |
| `Annotated[int, Ge(1), Le(100)]` *(control)* | `{"minimum": 1, "maximum": 100, ...}` | correct |

So `.ge(1).le(100).multiple_of(5)` publishes a schema advertising *any integer >= 1*, while the validator rejects 200 and 52. For FastAPI that means the OpenAPI component and every generated client disagree with the server.

### Cause

In `_apply_constraint()`, the `Ge`, `Lt` and `Le` branches apply their fallback function validator **unconditionally** - including when the native core-schema field was just set:

```python
elif isinstance(constraint, annotated_types.Ge):
    ge = constraint.ge
    if s and s['type'] in {'int', 'float', 'decimal'}:
        s = s.copy()
        if s['type'] == 'int' and isinstance(ge, int):
            s['ge'] = ge          # native constraint applied...
        ...

    def check_ge(v: Any) -> bool:
        return v >= ge

    s = _check_func(check_ge, f'>= {ge}', s)   # ...and then wrapped anyway
```

`_check_func` wraps the schema in `function-after`. The next constraint in the chain sees `s['type'] == 'function-after'`, which is not in `{'int', 'float', 'decimal'}`, so it cannot set its own native field and survives only inside an opaque callable that JSON-schema generation cannot read. Core schema for `.ge(1).le(100)`:

```
{'type': 'function-after',
 'function': ...,                       # <- le(100) lives in here, invisible to the schema
 'schema': {'type': 'function-after',
            'function': ...,            # <- redundant ge check
            'schema': {'type': 'int', 'ge': 1}}}
```

`Gt` is the control that works, and only by accident: its fallback sits in an `else:`, so nothing is wrapped when the native constraint applies.

### Relationship to the open PRs in this function

Two in-flight PRs each fix one branch of this, for unrelated reasons, and between them they leave `Ge`, `Lt` and `Le` untouched:

- **#13473** adds a `native_constraint_applied` flag to `MultipleOf` to avoid a float parity problem. Same shape as the fix needed here.
- **#13446** restructures `Gt` so the fallback lands inside the numeric branch.

Worth flagging on the second one: #13446's description argues that `Gt` is *uniquely* broken and holds up `Ge`/`Lt`/`Le`/`MultipleOf` as the correct model, because they "always apply" the check and so enforce the bound on a type mismatch. That is true of validation, but always applying it is exactly what destroys the schema. `Gt` is uniquely broken for validation; the other four are broken for schema. Whichever way this is fixed, it probably wants to be one symmetric change across all five branches rather than three separate patches.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import TypeAdapter
from pydantic.experimental.pipeline import validate_as

ta = TypeAdapter(Annotated[int, validate_as(int).ge(1).le(100)])

print(ta.json_schema())      # {'minimum': 1, 'type': 'integer'

title: RootModel.model_dump() typing signature rejects supported serialization arguments
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`RootModel` inherits the runtime implementation of `BaseModel.model_dump()`, but defines a separate declaration under `TYPE_CHECKING` to preserve its more precise return type.

That declaration has diverged from the base method:

- `context` is restricted to `dict[str, Any] | None` instead of `Any | None`.
- `fallback` is missing.
- `polymorphic_serialization` is missing.

As a result, Mypy, Pyright, and Pyrefly reject valid calls that succeed at runtime.

All three calls in the example below succeed at runtime.

Mypy currently reports errors equivalent to:

```text
Argument "context" to "model_dump" of "RootModel" has incompatible type "str"
Unexpected keyword argument "fallback" for "model_dump" of "RootModel"
Unexpected keyword argument "polymorphic_serialization" for "model_dump" of "RootModel"
```

Pyright and Pyrefly report the same signature incompatibilities.

## Expected behavior

The type-checking-only `RootModel.model_dump()` declaration should accept the same parameters, annotations, defaults, and ordering as `BaseModel.model_dump()`, while preserving the more precise `RootModel` return annotation.

## Cause

The declaration appears to have drifted as the base method evolved:

- Serialization context originally updated both signatures.
- `BaseModel.context` was later widened to `Any`.
- `fallback` was subsequently added to `BaseModel.model_dump()`.
- `polymorphic_serialization` was later added to `BaseModel.model_dump()`.

Those later changes were not propagated to the manually maintained `RootModel` declaration.

## Proposed fix

Update only the static `RootModel.model_dump()` signature and add focused regression cases to `tests/typechecking/root_model.py`.

No runtime serialization behavior needs to change.

I have prepared and locally validated a focused two-file fix. The following checks pass:

- Mypy type-checking suite
- Pyright type-checking suite
- Pyrefly type-checking suite
- Focused RootModel serialization tests
- Ruff lint and formatting checks
- `git diff --check`

I would be happy to submit the PR after the issue is reviewed and assigned.

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, RootModel, SerializationInfo, model_serializer


class ContextRoot(RootModel[str]):
    @model_serializer
    def serialize_root(self, info: SerializationInfo) -> str:
        return f'{info.context}:{self.root}'


class Unknown:
    pass


class Base(BaseModel):
    x: int


class Sub(Base):
    y: int


ContextRoot(root='value').model_dump(context='prefix')

RootModel[Any](root=Unknown()).model_dump(
    mode='json',
    fallback=lambda _: 'fallback',
)

RootModel[list[Base]](root=[Sub(x=1, y=2)]).model_dump(
    polymorphic_serialization=True,
)

title: `to_json` `temporal_mode="seconds"`/`"milliseconds"` ignores the timezone offset, producing a wrong unix timestamp for aware datetimes
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When serializing a timezone-aware `datetime` with `pydantic_core.to_json(..., temporal_mode="seconds")` (or `"milliseconds"`, or the `ser_json_temporal` config equivalent), the timezone offset is silently dropped. The wall-clock time is treated as if it were UTC, so the resulting unix timestamp is wrong by exactly the offset.

For example, `datetime(2026, 7, 9, 12, 0, 0, tzinfo=timezone(timedelta(hours=-5)))` represents the instant `2026-07-09T17:00:00Z` (unix `1783616400.0`), but `temporal_mode="seconds"` serializes it as `1783598400.0` — the same value as `12:00:00Z`. It should equal Python's `datetime.timestamp()`.

**Expected** (`temporal_mode="seconds"`):

| input | serialized seconds |
|---|---|
| `2026-07-09T12:00:00+00:00` | `1783598400.0` |
| `2026-07-09T12:00:00-05:00` | `1783616400.0` |

**Actual:**

| input | serialized seconds |
|---|---|
| `2026-07-09T12:00:00+00:00` | `1783598400.0` |
| `2026-07-09T12:00:00-05:00` | `1783598400.0` ❌ (offset dropped) |

By contrast, `temporal_mode="iso8601"` correctly preserves the offset (`"2026-07-09T12:00:00-05:00"`), so only the float/timestamp modes are affected.

**Root cause.** The float conversion sums the date's UTC-midnight timestamp with the *wall-clock* time-of-day and never applies `tz_offset` (`pydantic-core/src/serializers/type_serializers/datetime_etc.rs`

`datetime_to_milliseconds` / `time_to_milliseconds` have the same shape. `speedate`'s `Time` carries a `tz_offset`, but these functions ignore it. This has been present since the `seconds`/`milliseconds` temporal modes were introduced in [pydantic-core#1743](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1743)

### Example Code

```Python
import datetime
import pydantic_core

est = datetime.timezone(datetime.timedelta(hours=-5))
aware = datetime.datetime(2026, 7, 9, 12, 0, 0, tzinfo=est)  # == 2026-07-09T17:00:00Z

serialized = float(pydantic_core.to_json(aware, temporal_mode="seconds"))
correct = aware.timestamp()

print("pydantic seconds:", serialized)     # 1783598400.0
print("datetime.timestamp():", correct)    # 1783616400.0
print("iso8601 (correct):", pydantic_core.to_json(aware, temporal_mode="iso8601").decode())
#   "2026-07-09T12:00:00-05:00"  (offset preserved here)

assert serialized == correct, "temporal_mode='seconds' dropped the tz offset"
# AssertionError: 1783598400.0 != 1783616400.0
```

### Initial Checks

### Description

`tests/test_deprecated_field.py` has the following test (abridged):

```python
from typing_extensions import deprecated

def test_computed_field_deprecated():
    class Model(BaseModel):
        @computed_field(deprecated='This is deprecated')
        @property
        @deprecated('This is deprecated (this message is overridden)')
        def p2(self) -> int:
            return 1

    instance = Model()

    pytest.warns(DeprecationWarning, lambda: instance.p2, match='^This is deprecated$')
```

But you can see by executing the same code in a REPL that this doesn't actually work as intended:

Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.

title: 'fraction_validator' raises unhandled 'ZeroDivisionError' for zero-denominator string input instead of 'ValidationError'
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

**Bug description**

The `fraction_validator` in `pydantic/_internal/_validators.py` only catches `ValueError` when constructing a `fractions.Fraction` from user input. However, Python's standard `fractions.Fraction` raises `ZeroDivisionError` when the denominator is zero (e.g., the string `"6/0"`). Because this exception is not caught, it bubbles up as a raw Python exception instead of being converted into a `ValidationError`, violating Pydantic's contract that all invalid user input should result in a `ValidationError`.

This was discovered during fuzzing of `TypeAdapter.validate_strings()` with the Atheris fuzzer.

**Expected behavior**

A `pydantic.ValidationError` should be raised with a message indicating that the input is not a valid fraction.

**Actual behavior**

```python
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../pydantic/_internal/_validators.py", line 253, in fraction_validator
    return Fraction(input_value)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File ".../fractions.py", line 281, in __new__
    raise ZeroDivisionError('Fraction(%s, 0)' % numerator)
ZeroDivisionError: Fraction(6, 0)
```

**Root cause**

In `pydantic/_internal/_validators.py`, line 247-254:

```python
def fraction_validator(input_value: Any, /) -> Fraction:
    if isinstance(input_value, Fraction):
        return input_value

    try:
        return Fraction(input_value)
    except ValueError:
        raise PydanticCustomError('fraction_parsing', 'Input is not a valid fraction')
```

The `except` clause only catches `ValueError`, but `Fraction("6/0")` raises `ZeroDivisionError`.

**Proposed fix**

Add `ZeroDivisionError` to the exception tuple:

```diff
--- a/pydantic/_internal/_validators.py
+++ b/pydantic/_internal/_validators.py
@@ -250,7 +250,7 @@ def fraction_validator(input_value: Any, /) -> Fraction:
 
     try:
         return Fraction(input_value)
-    except ValueError:
+    except (ValueError, ZeroDivisionError):
         raise PydanticCustomError('fraction_parsing', 'Input is not a valid fraction')
```

This is consistent with how other validators in the same file handle exceptions from standard library constructors (e.g., `decimal_validator`, `uuid_validator`, `ip_*_validators`).

The bug exists and not fixed in 'main' branch as well.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import TypeAdapter
import fractions

adapter = TypeAdapter(fractions.Fraction)

# This should raise ValidationError, but raises ZeroDivisionError
adapter.validate_strings("6/0")
```

title: __slots__ is not propagated to generic parameterizations, silently re-adding __weakref__
body:
## Description

`BaseModel.__class_getitem__` synthesizes a new class for each parameterization (`Model[X]`) via `pydantic/_internal/_generics.py::create_generic_submodel`. That function builds the class with a namespace containing only `__module__` (plus what `prepare_class` adds) and never forwards `__slots__` from `origin`. Because the new class body has no `__slots__`, Python's class machinery adds the default `__dict__` and `__weakref__` descriptors. The parent's `__slots__ = ()` is silently discarded for every parameterization.

## Reproducer

```python
import weakref
import pydantic

class Envelope[T](pydantic.BaseModel):
    __slots__ = ()
    content: None | T = None

base = Envelope()
print("base __weakref__:", "__weakref__" in type(base).__dict__)       # False - good
weakref.ref(base)                                                       # TypeError - good

param = Envelope[int]()
print("param __weakref__:", "__weakref__" in type(param).__dict__)     # True  - unexpected
weakref.ref(param)                                                      # succeeds - unexpected

# Even an explicit subclass with __slots__ = () cannot recover, because
# the auto-synthesized intermediate already carries __weakref__:
class Sub(Envelope[int]):
    __slots__ = ()
weakref.ref(Sub())                                                      # succeeds
```

## Expected

`Envelope[int]` (and any user subclass of it) should honor the `__slots__ = ()` declared on the origin and reject `weakref.ref(...)`, matching the un-parameterized `Envelope`.

## Actual

The synthesized `Envelope[int]` class has neither `__slots__` in its own dict nor any inherited declaration that suppresses default storage, so `__weakref__` (and `__dict__`, but `BaseModel` itself forces that one) reappears on every parameterized subclass and on anything inheriting from it.

## Root cause

`pydantic/_internal/_generics.py::create_generic_submodel` constructs the class with:

```python
namespace: dict[str, Any] = {"__module__": origin.__module__}
bases = (origin,)
meta, ns, kwds = prepare_class(model_name, bases)
namespace.update(ns)
created_model = meta(model_name, bases, namespace, ...)
```

`__slots__` is never copied from `origin` into `namespace`, so the synthesized class is declared without it.

## Suggested fix

```python
namespace: dict[str, Any] = {"__module__": origin.__module__}
if "__slots__" in origin.__dict__:
    namespace["__slots__"] = origin.__slots__
```

This propagates the origin's slot declaration to every parameterization. Models that intentionally omit `__slots__` are unaffected. Models that declare `__slots__` (including the common `__slots__ = ()` to drop `__weakref__`) get the behavior they asked for on `Model[X]` as well as on `Model`.

## Workaround

Replace the runtime generic with a `typing.Protocol[T]` and have each concrete envelope inherit `BaseModel` directly. The Protocol parameterization is typing-only, so no intermediate class is synthesized and the concrete classes' `__slots__ = ()` is respected. Costs the parent's shared fields in duplication across concrete subclasses.

## Versions

- pydantic 2.13.4
- Python 3.13

title: Cannot use `None` as type argument
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Pydantic's BaseModel.__class_getitem__ is annotated as `typevar_values: type[Any] | tuple[type[Any], ...]`, which causes type checkers to reject `None` as a type argument even though `None` is a valid PEP 484 type
annotation meaning `type(None)` / `NoneType`.

Error in PyCharm: `Expected type 'type | tuple[type, ...]', got 'type[None]'`

Root cause: pydantic/main.py BaseModel.__class_getitem__ signature should accept
`None` (and other special forms) as valid type arguments, not just `type[Any]`.

We could use `NoneType` to get rid of the problem, however, I suggest we update annotation on pydantic side.

### Example Code

```Python
import pydantic as p


class Box[T](p.BaseModel):
    pass


# Triggers the warning because Pydantic's __class_getitem__ is typed as
# typevar_values: type[Any] | tuple[type[Any], ...]
# and None is not type[Any]:
x = Box[None]()
```

title: Nit about validator documentation code sample
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

This is strictly a documentation related issue.


The code sample here: https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/2.3/usage/validators#model-validators has a function `check_passwords_match` that tests if the fields are `None`.  These tests are unnecessary in this context as the fields are not `Optional`.  Including these tests makes the code sample gives the impression that the password fields to be `None` when in fact they cannot due to the design of pydantic.

# Reproduce the error

Include the following additional code snippet at the bottom of the example code:
```
bad = UserModel(username="bad", password1=None, password2=None)
```
and execute the script.  You'll see that you get validation errors on the password fields /before the custom validator is run/.


# Proposed fix

Remove the (uneccessary) None checks from the validator function:

```
 @model_validator(mode="after")                                                                                      
 def check_passwords_match(self) -> "UserModel":                                                                     
        pw1 = self.password1                                                                                            
        pw2 = self.password2                                                                                            
        if pw1 != pw2:                                                                                                  
            raise ValueError("passwords do not match")                                                                  
        return self e validator function to be

```
Optional:  include a comment that they cannot be None due to the pydantic intrinsic type validation that is run prior to the execution of the custom validator.

title: pydantic-core macOS wheels break Homebrew install on macOS 15 (-headerpad_max_install_names)
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

macOS 15 CI runners use Apple's new linker (`ld_prime`), which reserves significantly less Mach-O header padding than the old `ld`. Homebrew's post-install fixup (`install_name_tool`) needs that padding to rewrite dylib paths after installation. When it's absent, `brew install`/`brew upgrade` fails for any formula that vendors `pydantic-core`.

**Error:**
```
Error: Failed changing dylib ID of
  .../pydantic_core/_pydantic_core.cpython-311-darwin.so
Updated load commands do not fit in the header of
  .../_pydantic_core.cpython-311-darwin.so
...needs to be relinked, possibly with -headerpad or -headerpad_max_install_names
```

**Fix:** three lines in `pydantic-core/build.rs`, gated to macOS:

```rust
if std::env::var("CARGO_CFG_TARGET_OS").as_deref() == Ok("macos") {
    println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg=-Wl,-headerpad_max_install_names");
}
```

`cargo:rustc-link-arg` passes the flag directly to the final `cdylib` link step, covering published wheels, source builds, and downstream Homebrew formulas.

The same root cause and fix is being addressed in `pyca/cryptography`: https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/pull/14777

A branch with the fix is ready at `washingtoneg/pydantic:fix/macos-headerpad-max-install-names`.

title: RootModel JSON schema drops examples from root field FieldInfo in 2.13
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

In Pydantic 2.13, `Field(examples=...)` on a `RootModel` root type is no longer surfaced in the generated JSON schema. This worked in 2.12.

The `FieldInfo` correctly stores the examples value, and `TypeAdapter` with the same type produces the correct schema — only `RootModel.model_json_schema()` drops it.

### Example Code

```Python
import json
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import Field, RootModel, TypeAdapter

MyType = Annotated[str, Field(examples=["hello", "world"])]

class MyModel(RootModel[MyType]):
    pass

# examples MISSING
print(json.dumps(MyModel.model_json_schema(), indent=2))
# {"title": "MyModel", "type": "string"}

# examples PRESENT with TypeAdapter
print(json.dumps(TypeAdapter(MyType).json_schema(), indent=2))
# {"examples": ["hello", "world"], "type": "string"}

# FieldInfo has the data — it's just not surfaced in the schema
print(MyModel.model_fields['root'].examples)
# ['hello', 'world']
```

## Expected output from `model_json_schema()`:

```json
json{
  "examples": ["hello", "world"],
  "title": "MyModel",
  "type": "string"
}
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text
Python 3.14.4
Pydantic 2.13.0
Works in Pydantic 2.12.5
```

title: # SIGSEGV at shutdown (`Py_FinalizeEx` / GC): Django + pydantic-core (Python 3.12)
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Maybe Related: [pydantic#12867](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/12867).

## Summary

When running Django’s test runner inside a Docker CI image with **`pydantic`** /
**`pydantic-core`** pins in the **2.11+** line, the **test suite reports success**, then
the **Python process segfaults during teardown** while the interpreter is shutting down
(**garbage collection** → **`Py_FinalizeEx`**).

Under **`gdb`**, the crashing thread shows **three frames inside**
**`pydantic_core/_pydantic_core.cpython-312-…so`** immediately above **`datetime_dealloc`**
in **`_datetime.cpython-312-…so`**. That matches the **shutdown / datetime /
pydantic-core** pattern discussed in **#12867** (the issue’s Python 3.11 trace includes
**`TzInfo`** / **`_Py_Dealloc`**).

We do **not** have a minimal public repro without our application code; this report
documents **versions**, **symptoms**, **`gdb`** capture, and **how we run tests** so
maintainers can compare with **#12867** and decide whether this is the same root cause on
**Python 3.12**.

---

## Environment

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| OS / image | Rocky Linux 9–style container (`test-django` in our repo) |
| Python | **3.12** |
| Packages (repro) | **`pydantic==2.13.2`**, **`pydantic-core==2.46.2`** (`pip -U` in image) |
| Runner | Django **`manage.py test`** with Postgres + Redis (Compose) |
| Baseline (stable in our runs) | **`pydantic==2.10.6`**, **`pydantic-core==2.27.2`** |

---

## Expected vs actual

**Expected:** After tests finish, the process exits with code **0** and the interpreter
shuts down cleanly.

**Actual:**

- Tests print **`OK`** and normal Django teardown (including **`Flushing redis…`**).
- Then either:
  - **`Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault`** (stderr), often **`Garbage-collecting`**
    with no Python frame; exit **139**, or
  - Under **`gdb`**: **`SIGSEGV`** with the stack below.

The failure happens **after** tests succeed, during **finalization / GC**, not during
assertions.

---

## Reproduction notes (our stack)

These steps assume our monorepo layout (`/myapp` in the container). They are **not** a
fully self-contained upstream repro; they show how we trigger the crash.

1. Start Compose (from our `docker/` dir): **`test-django`** with healthy Postgres
   and Redis.
2. Upgrade pins (example): `pip install -U 'pydantic==2.13.2'` (pulls
   **`pydantic-core==2.46.2`**).
3. Run **`manage.py test`** against a subset that imports **Pydantic `BaseModel`** (we used
   `myapp.dashboards.models.tests.test_build`).
4. Invoke **`python …/manage.py`** with the same
   **`LD_LIBRARY_PATH`** as **`./manage`** (via **`.environment`**); otherwise unrelated
   native imports fail before Django starts.

**Docker / `gdb`:**

- **`--cap-add=SYS_PTRACE`** on **`docker compose run`** so **`gdb`** can run the inferior.
- Debug with **`gdb --args /myapp/manage.py test …`**
  (interpreter + **`manage.py`**); do not run **`gdb`** on **`python`** alone.

---

## GDB stack trace (abbreviated — Python 3.12)

Fault thread (**Thread 1**). Other threads were idle OpenBLAS helpers.

```text

Fault thread is **Thread 1** (main); other threads are idle OpenBLAS workers.

```text
Thread 1 "python" received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
0x00007fb959a5662d in ?? () from /myapp/.venv/lib64/python3.12/site-packages/pydantic_core/_pydantic_core.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so

Thread 7 (Thread 0x7fb94b9fd640 (LWP 91) "python"):
#0  0x00007fb96a63737a in __futex_abstimed_wait_common () from /lib64/libc.so.6
No symbol table info available.
#1  0x00007fb96a6398d2 in pthread_cond_wait@@GLIBC_2.3.2 () from /lib64/libc.so.6
No symbol table info available.
#2  0x00007fb955dca3eb in blas_thread_server () from .../scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-....so
...

title: Model field name shadowing model class name breaks Optional nested model parsing
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When a BaseModel field name is identical to the referenced model class name, Pydantic fails to correctly parse the nested model if it is optional.

### Example Code
The following example does not work as expected:

```python
from typing import Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Address(BaseModel):
    street: str

class School(BaseModel):
    name: str
    Address: Optional[Address] = None

if __name__ == '__main__':
    entry = {"name": "Example name", "Address": {"street": "Example street"}}
    s = School(**entry)
    print(f"{s = }")
```


It only works when slightly modifying the Address class name like the following:
```python
from typing import Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel

class _Address(BaseModel):
    street: str

class School(BaseModel):
    name: str
    Address: Optional[_Address] = None

if __name__ == '__main__':

title: Regression on Python 3.12: from_attributes=True now raises get_attribute_error for optional nested fields when attribute access raises an AttributeError subclass
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

 I found a behavior change between Pydantic 2.12 and 2.13 when validating objects with from_attributes=True.

 For an optional nested field, if attribute access raises a subclass of AttributeError, Pydantic 2.12 treats that as a missing attribute and sets the field to None, while Pydantic 2.13
 raises a ValidationError with type='get_attribute_error'.

 Interestingly, I can reproduce this on Python 3.12, but not on Python 3.13.

 This matters in Django because reverse one-to-one missing relations raise RelatedObjectDoesNotExist, which is a subclass of AttributeError.

### Example Code


#### Repro on Python 3.12 with Pydantic 2.12

 ```bash
   uvx --python 3.12 --with "pydantic~=2.12.0" python - <<'PY'
   import pydantic
   from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

title: Decimal JSON schema pattern rejects pydantic's own scientific notation serialization output (v2.12 regression)
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

**`model_json_schema(mode="serialization")` pattern for `Decimal` breaks on scientific notation**

The serialization schema for `Decimal` fields generates a regex that rejects values that `model_dump_json()` itself produces.

Specifically: `pydantic-core`'s serializer calls `str()` on `Decimal` objects, which outputs scientific notation for small/large values. E.g. `Decimal('0.0000001')` becomes `"1E-7"`. But the pattern added in #11987 (`^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\d*\.?\d*$`) has no `[eE]` component, so it'll never match those strings.

As a result, any downstream consumer validating `model_dump_json()` output against `model_json_schema()`, such as OpenAPI validators and codegen + validation tools like Orval + Zod, will intermittently reject perfectly valid serialized values. Intermittent because only certain `Decimal` values trigger scientific notation.

**v2.11**:
```json
{"anyOf": [{"type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}]}
```

**v2.12**:
```json
{"anyOf": [{"pattern": "^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\\d*\\.?\\d*$", "type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}]}
```

Two possible fixes:
- Append `(?:[eE][+-]?\d+)?` to the pattern in serialization mode
- Normalize `Decimal` to fixed-point during serialization before it ever hits the schema

### Example Code

```Python
import json
import re
from decimal import Decimal
from pydantic import BaseModel

class MyModel(BaseModel):
    value: Decimal | None

schema = MyModel.model_json_schema(mode="serialization")
pattern = next(
    v for v in schema["properties"]["value"]["anyOf"] if v.get("type") == "string"
)["pattern"]
regex = re.compile(pattern)

# pydantic serializes this as "1E-7" which fails its own schema's pattern
m = MyModel(value=Decimal("0.0000001"))
serialized = json.loads(m.model_dump_json())["value"]

print(f"Pattern: {pattern}")
print(f"Serialized: {serialized!r}")
print(f"Matches: {bool(regex.match(serialized))}")
# Pattern: ^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\d*\.?\d*$
# Serialized: '1E-7'
# Matches: False
```

title: Overriding `extra` causes `BaseModel` equality to fail
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Take this simple reproducer
```python
class A(BaseModel, extra="allow"):
    a: int

A(a=1) == A.model_validate({"a": 1})   # True
A(a=1) == A.model_validate({"a": 1}, extra="forbid")   # False
```
So, just the fact that we forbid extra fields in the second example cause the equality to fail, even though the field values are identical and we didn't actually pass in any extra fields.

This appears to be because `A(a=1).model_extra == {}` and `A.model_validate({"a": 1}, extra="forbid").model_extra is None`. This check needs to be extended so that model extra being `{}` vs `None` still counts as being equal

title: ConfigDict accepts unknown keys without warning — typos like stric=True silently ignored
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`ConfigDict` accepts any key without validation. A typo like `stric=True` (missing the `t`) is silently accepted - `strict` is never set, and no warning is emitted. The developer gets no signal that their configuration has no effect.

Pydantic validates everything else - field types, annotations, aliases. `ConfigDict` is the one place where an invalid key passes through without any check. A `logging.warning` on unrecognized keys would catch typos and removed/renamed settings early.

I found this by systematically scoring enforcement levels across pydantic's config propagation pipeline. The invariant analysis methodology is documented at [github.com/savarin/lean-agent](https://github.com/savarin/lean-agent). I have a working fix (`pydantic/_internal/_config.py`, ~11 lines) and can open a PR immediately if this is something the team wants.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class MyModel(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(stric=True)  # typo: should be 'strict'
    name: str

m = MyModel(name="alice")
print(f"model_config: {MyModel.model_config}")
print(f"strict actually set: {MyModel.model_config.get('strict', 'NOT SET')}")
print(f"stric (typo) present: {'stric' in MyModel.model_config}")
# model_config: {'stric': True}
# strict actually set: NOT SET
# stric (typo) present: True
# — zero warnings emitted

title: Decimal JSON schema pattern uses lookahead regex unsupported by pydantic-core
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

  Pydantic v2 emits a JSON schema for Decimal fields that includes a regex pattern with a negative lookahead `((?!...))`. This pattern cannot be compiled by `pydantic-core`'s Rust regex crate, which does not support look-around assertions.

  This means the JSON schema pydantic produces for Decimal cannot be round-tripped back through pydantic's own validation  e.g. constructing a `TypeAdapter` with `StringConstraints(pattern=...)` using the emitted pattern fails with a `SchemaError`.

  This is a practical problem for any tooling that reconstructs pydantic types from emitted JSON schemas (e.g. MCP structured content parsing via FastMCP).


### Example Code

```Python
"""Minimal reproduction: Decimal JSON schema pattern uses lookahead unsupported by pydantic-core.

Pydantic generates a JSON schema for Decimal fields with a regex pattern that uses
a negative lookahead (?!...). When that schema is round-tripped back through pydantic
(e.g. via TypeAdapter with StringConstraints), pydantic-core's Rust regex engine
rejects it because it does not support look-around assertions.
"""

from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, StringConstraints, TypeAdapter


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    amount: Decimal


def test_decimal_json_schema_pattern_roundtrips_through_pydantic_core():
    schema = MyModel.model_json_schema()

    # Decimal emits an anyOf with a string variant carrying the pattern
    string_variant = next(v for v in schema['properties']['amount']['anyOf'] if v.get('type') == 'string')
    pattern = string_variant['pattern']

    # The emitted pattern contains a negative lookahead:
    assert '(?!' in pattern

    # Feeding it back into StringConstraints fails with:
    #   SchemaError: regex parse error: look-around ... is not supported
    ConstrainedStr = Annotated[str, StringConstraints(pattern=pattern)]
    TypeAdapter(ConstrainedStr)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    test_decimal_json_schema_pattern_roundtrips_through_pydantic_core()
```

title: Subclass Serialization Includes Child Fields with MISSING Sentinel
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

# Pydantic Bug Report: Subclass Serialization Includes Child Fields with MISSING Sentinel

## Summary

When a base class contains fields with `| MISSING` type annotation AND a container field uses `| MISSING` in its union type, Pydantic fails to properly serialize subclasses according to their declared parent type. Instead, it serializes the full runtime (child) type, including fields that should be excluded.

## Versions

- **pydantic**: 2.12.5
- **pydantic_core**: 2.41.5

## Minimal Reproducer

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, TypeAdapter
from pydantic.experimental.missing_sentinel import MISSING

class Base(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra='forbid')
    base_field: str | MISSING = MISSING  # Key ingredient 1

class Parent(Base):
    parent_field: str

class Child(Parent):
    child_field: str  # Should NOT appear when serializing as Parent

class Container(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra='forbid')
    item: Parent | MISSING = MISSING  # Key ingredient 2

# Create child and assign to parent-typed field
child = Child(parent_field='p', child_field='c')
container = Container(item=child)

# Serialize
result = TypeAdapter(Container).dump_python(container, mode='json')

# Expected: {'item': {'parent_field': 'p'}}
# Actual:   {'item': {'parent_field': 'p', 'child_field': 'c'}}
print(f"Has child_field (BUG): {'child_field' in result.get('item', {})}")  # True (incorrect)
```

## Control Tests

The issue **only** occurs when **both** conditions are met:

### Without MISSING in base class - Works correctly

```python
class BaseNoMissing(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra='forbid')
    base_field: str = ''  # Not MISSING

class ParentNoMissing(BaseNoMissing):
    parent_field: str

class ChildNoMissing(ParentNoMissing):
    child_field: str

class ContainerControl1(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra='forbid')
    item: ParentNoMissing | MISSING = MISSING

child1 = ChildNoMissing(parent_field='p', child_field='c')
container1 = ContainerControl1(item=child1)
result1 = TypeAdapter(ContainerControl1).dump_python(container1, mode='json')
print(f"Without MISSING in base: has child_field = {'child_field' in result1.get('item', {})}")  # False (correct)
```

### Without MISSING in container field union - Works correctly

```python
class ContainerControl2(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra='forbid')
    item: Parent  # No MISSING union

child2 = Child(parent_field='p', child_field='c')
container2 = ContainerControl2(item=child2)
result2 = TypeAdapter(ContainerControl2).dump_python(container2, mode='json')
print(f"Without MISSING in container: has child_field = {'child_field' in result2.get('item', {})}")  # False (correct)
```

### Using None instead of MISSING - Works correctly

```python
class ContainerWithNone(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra='forbid')
    item: Parent | None = None

child3 = Child(parent_field='p', child_field='c')
container3 = ContainerWithNone(item=child3)
result3 = TypeAdapter(ContainerWithNone).dump_python(container3, mode='json')
print(f"With None instead of MISSING: has child_field = {'child_field' in result3.get('item', {})}")  # False (correct)
```

## Expected Behavior

When serializing a child class instance through a field typed as the parent class, Pydantic should only serialize fields defined in the declared type (parent), excluding fields added by subclasses.

## Actual Behavior

When both a base class in the inheritance chain has `| MISSING` fields AND the container field uses `| MISSING` union, Pydantic serializes all fields from the runtime type, including child-specific fields that should be excluded.

## Impact

This breaks type safety in APIs where the response schema declares a parent type but the implementation may return subclasses. Clients receive unexpected extra fields that violate the API contract.

## Workaround

title: `to_json`: `timedelta_mode` and `temporal_mode` break documented behavior
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`pydantic_core.to_json` (and `to_jsonable_python`) documents `timedelta_mode` and `temporal_mode` as independent parameters governing disjoint type sets:

> - `timedelta_mode`: How to serialize `timedelta` objects, either `'iso8601'` or `'float'`.
> - `temporal_mode`: How to serialize datetime-like objects (`datetime`, `date`, `time`), either `'iso8601'`, `'seconds'`, or `'milliseconds'`.

(This is what both the [API docs](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/api/pydantic-core/pydantic_core/) and the shipped `_pydantic_core.pyi` type stub say.)

Given that contract, `to_json(..., timedelta_mode="float", temporal_mode="iso8601")` should serialize `datetime`/`date`/`time` as ISO 8601 strings and `timedelta` as a float. Instead, `datetime`/`date`/`time` are **also** coerced to unix-timestamp floats, `timedelta_mode="float"` silently overrides `temporal_mode="iso8601"` for all temporal types.

There is no combination of the two parameters that yields ISO datetimes with float-second timedeltas, even though the documented parameters imply there should be.

**Root cause / regression.** This regressed in [#1743](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1743). Before that PR, `SerializationConfig` had a dedicated `timedelta_mode: TimedeltaMode` field and `to_json` had no `temporal_mode` parameter, so `timedelta_mode` was genuinely independent. #1743 replaced the dedicated field with a single unified `temporal_mode` and retrofitted `timedelta_mode` as a legacy alias that maps into it.

Either the docs/`.pyi` should be corrected to state that `timedelta_mode` is a deprecated alias that affects all temporal types, or (preferably) `timedelta` should retain an independent setting so the documented behavior holds. Personally I have a requirement to be able to set the `timedelta` format independent of the other `datetime` types.

### Example Code

```Python
import datetime
import pydantic_core

payload = {
    "dt": datetime.datetime(2026, 7, 9, 12, 0, 0),
    "d": datetime.date(2026, 7, 9),

title: docs: timedelta spec string is incorrect
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

The documentation for the accepted timedelta formats seems wrong or outdated: https://docs.pydantic.dev/2.9/api/standard_library_types/#datetimetimedelta

While I assume the ISO format parsing works fine, I was interested in the alternate format listed:
`[-][DD]D[,][HH:MM:]SS[.ffffff]`

With the current docs giving the following examples:
- `1d,01:02:03.000004`
- `1D01:02:03.000004`
- `01:02:03`

Let's examine some definite discrepancies:
1. The example `01:02:03` doesn't satisfy the mandatory `D` in the spec string.
2. From that example and the spec (`[HH:MM:]SS`) I'd expect to be able use just `12` to mean 12 seconds. That doesn't work.

I suspect `[-][[DD]D,]HH:MM:SS[.ffffff]` more closely reflects what's currently accepted, although i haven't rigurously verified it.

Also, mixing the same letters for digit placeholders and literals here (e.g. `D`) makes for bad readability, but maybe there's a technical reason for it?

### Example Code

```Python
import pydantic

from datetime import timedelta


class Model(pydantic.BaseModel):
    td: timedelta


# docs:  [-][DD]D[,][HH:MM:]SS[.ffffff]


# let's run through the doc examples first.
for s in [
  '1d,01:02:03.000004',
  '1D01:02:03.000004',
  '01:02:03',
]:
    # all of these do work correctly.
    assert Model(td=s)


worked = {}
# i would expect at least one of these to work
for s in [
    "1",
    "01",
    "12",
    "12.123456",
    "012",
    "112",
    "D12",
    "0,12",
    "0d12",
    "0d,12",
    "1,12",
    "1d12",
    "1d,12",
    "12D12",
    "12312",
    "1,12s",
    "1d12s",
    "1d,12s",
]:
    try:
        worked[s] = Model(td=s)
    except Exception as ex:
        print(f"Failed to parse {s!r}:\n{ex}\n")

# but it doesn't
assert not worked
```

title: The docs should treat "FieldValidatorModes" more clearly, as they do for Model Validator Modes ("Literal['wrap', 'before', 'after']")
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [X] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Hi, thanks for the incredible work on this library! 

### The Problem

I was recently implementing some Field Validators for the first time, and the docs are frustratingly vague when it comes to the modes -- the tutorial doesn't give any examples for modes other than the default, and reference doesn't even say what the options are ([before, after, wrap, plain](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/19f7d414c58d6af544f39c3e4a0e62b0dca6ab7f/pydantic/functional_validators.py#L392)), instead just giving the name of the convenience typedef "FieldValidatorModes". There's some great discussion for *model* validator modes, but A) it should be in both places or linked from one to the other, and B) there's no discussion whatsoever of the "plain" type, since it's only available for field validators. Which is extra confusing because the default is "after", not "plain"! 

### The Solution

Assuming I didn't miss the documentation (super possible), I think the change here should primarily be a documentation one (specifically to [`/api/functional_validators`](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/functional_validators/#pydantic.functional_validators.model_validator) and [`/concepts/validators`](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/validators/#field-validators)). 

One could argue that the direct, typedef-less approach from @adriangb's April 2023 [commit implementing ModelValidator](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/commit/7232fadc3e2f9f38497e47216e0da311f23339bb#diff-ca272dc261af03011fed42df0a75b39dec2bd2710419a7c7bcfb54cc69bca8b6R128) could/should be applied to FieldValidator too, but that's obviously only an internal concern. **At the very least, I would passionately request:**

1. Listing the four options in the docs somewhere instead of/in addition to the typedef name
2. An explanation of the "plain" mode
3. And a clarification that the function signature does not change for `field_validator(mode="before")` / `field_validator(mode="after")` like it does for `model_validator(mode="before")` / `model_validator(mode="after")`.**

I'd offer to help out myself / propose a pull request, but I don't have time to setup your dev system, so I'm leaving this instead. Will try to come back to it sometime if y'all are too busy :)

title: model_validator mode="before" applied in the wrong order (from current class to base)
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

In pydantic v1, if we declared a root_validator with pre=True in Base model and in a subclass, it would first call the base root validator, and then the subclass one. It makes sense to e.g. customize some logic in all models

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, root_validator


class Base(BaseModel):
    x: int
    y: str

    @root_validator(pre=True)
    @classmethod
    def base_validator(cls, values):
        print("CALL 1")
        values["x"] = 1
        return values


class Model(Base):

    @root_validator(pre=True)
    @classmethod
    def model_validator(cls, values):
        print("CALL 2")
        values["x"] = 2
        return values


model = Model(x=3, y="a")

print(model)
```

Outputs first CALL 1, then CALL 2, as expected

But in pydantic v2, it's vice versa: first the subclass model_validator is called, and only then in BaseModel. It's counter-intuitive

Maybe there's a way to workaround this, but I was using it to workaround another issue: when using from_attributes=True, `model_validator` with `mode="before"` receives a model object instead of a dictionary, so my custom logic doesn't expect this and I need to make the same conversions pydantic-core does here: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/blob/bb67044c67b705d3ac7990ef067deb786e8d5afe/src/input/return_enums.rs#L293-L331

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator


class Base(BaseModel):
    x: int
    y: str

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def base_validator(cls, values):
        print("CALL 1")
        values["x"] = 1
        return values


class Model(Base):

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def model_validator(cls, values):
        print("CALL 2")
        values["x"] = 2
        return values


model = Model(x=3, y="a")

print(model)
```

title: Clarification Needed: Differentiation Between Types and Constraints in Documentation
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Hey there!

I've been working with Pydantic and came across something a bit confusing in the documentation.
I noticed that some types listed in the [Pydantic Types documentation](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/types/#pydantic.types.StringConstraints) are actually data classes, like `StringConstraints`. While types like `PositiveInt` work as expected when used directly, trying to use `StringConstraints` as a type throws an error.

Here’s a small example:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError, StringConstraints

class Model(BaseModel):
    name: StringConstraints(to_lower=True, strip_whitespace=True)

try:
    print(Model(name="Aa    "))
except ValidationError as ex:
    print(ex)
```

This gives me:

```
AttributeError: 'StringConstraints' object has no attribute '__mro__'
```

However, using `Annotated` works fine:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, StringConstraints
from typing import Annotated
 
class Model(BaseModel):
    name: Annotated[str, StringConstraints(to_lower=True, strip_whitespace=True)]
```

So, my understanding is that `StringConstraints` is not actually a type but more like metadata or constraints. But listing it alongside actual types like `PositiveInt` in the documentation is a bit misleading.

It would be super helpful if the docs could clarify this a bit more—maybe add a hint that data classes like `StringConstraints` need to be used with `Annotated` and aren’t meant to be used as direct types.

Thanks a lot!

body:

The docs for `BaseModel.model_validate_json` state that it raises `ValueError` If `json_data` is not a JSON string (https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/pydantic/main.py#L592).

title: Dataclass ConfigDict frozen doesn't work as expected
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

There are two apparent ways to make a dataclass frozen. Coming from using ordinary class-based Pydantic models to dataclass-based ones, I found myself providing ConfigDict(frozen=True) to the dataclass decorator. However, this doesn't work with dataclasses, instead you have to provide this argument to the decorator.

This could be made clearer in the docs, one of the arguments could be removed (pref the ConfigDict one), or the dataclass could default to either of which is set (would be a problem if both were set to opposite values).

Cheers!

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import ConfigDict
from pydantic.dataclasses import dataclass

# Throws error:

@dataclass(config=ConfigDict(frozen=True))
class Location:
    latitude: float
    longitude: float

location = Location(latitude=0, longitude=0)
hash(location)
# TypeError: unhashable type: 'Location'


# Works:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Location:
    latitude: float
    longitude: float

location = Location(latitude=0, longitude=0)
hash(location)

title: Inconsistent behavior with extra configuration when inheriting from multiple models between pydantic v1 and v2
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

I am migrating from Pydantic v1 to v2 and have encountered some inconsistencies and validation issues, particularly with the `extra` configuration options (`extra='ignore'` and `extra='forbid'`). 

My observations:
**Import Order Dependency:** The order of imports matters when inheriting from multiple model classes, which is typical Python behavior but crucial to note during migration.
**Configuration Changes:** In Pydantic v1, similar configurations lead to different behaviors compared to Pydantic v2. The shift from using class-based configuration to the `model_config` attribute in v2 appears to be the root of these discrepancies.

I'm unsure if these differences are due to a bug or are intended changes in the new version.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel
import pydantic

print("Python version:", sys.version)

title: [docs]: cannot leverage on alias_priority if alias_generator is not involved
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Hi everybody,
first off, thank you for your amazing work on `pydantic` and on the other products!

I would like to point out a possible (I apologize if this is not the case and I'm missing something) inconsistency in the documentation at https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/fields/#field-aliases, where the note specifies that 

> !!! note "Alias precedence and priority"
      In case you use `alias` together with `validation_alias` or `serialization_alias` at the same time,
      the `validation_alias` will have priority over `alias` for validation, and `serialization_alias` will have priority
      over `alias` for serialization.

> **You may also set `alias_priority` on a field to change this behavior.**

As far as I could experiment, there's no way you can leverage on `alias_priority` if you don't use an `AliasGenerator`. If that's effectively the case, IMO the final statement in the note might be somewhat misleading because the section does not deal with alias generators, whose _alias precedence_ behaviours are indeed well described at https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/alias/#alias-precedence.

As a possible corroboration to that, tests at `pydantic/tests/test_aliases.py` do not reference `alias_priority` when an `AliasGenerator` is not involved (if not for testing that `alias_priority=2` by default when `repr`esenting a model).

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Model(BaseModel):
    first_name: str = Field(
        alias="firstName",
        validation_alias="FIRST_NAME",
        serialization_alias="f_name",
        alias_priority=1
    )


model = Model(firstName="Pippo")   # ValidationError, no way to tweak alias_priority to be able to validate via plain_alias
print(model.model_dump())
print(model.model_dump(by_alias=True))   # Serialization via serialization_alias only
```

### Initial Checks

### Description

When I have a parent and child class that both implement `model_validator`, the parent's model validator is ignored in the child class. 

This can be a source of bugs as one might expect the parent's validation to run together with the child's validation.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator

class Sub(BaseModel):
    positive: int

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    @classmethod

            raise ValueError()
        return v

class Main(Sub):

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    @classmethod
    def model_validator(cls, v):
        if v.negative >= 0:

title: ValidationError Input should be None when field is named as type inside Optional
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

I've encountered a strange `ValidationError` while using a model with a `bytes` field and an `Optional[bytes]` annotation.

Please consider the examples below. 

It seems the issue is not with using a built-in type as a field name (which is doubtful but okay), but rather with the fact that the field name and the type inside `Optional` are the same.

I've also seen closed https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/7871, but the problem presents in the latest version of `pydantic`.

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Optional

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

# OK
class M1(BaseModel):
    payload: Optional[str] = None


m1 = M1(payload='123')

# OK
class M2(BaseModel):
    payload: Optional[bytes] = None


m2 = M2(payload=b'123')

# Bug
class M3(BaseModel):
    str: Optional[str] = None


try:
    m3 = M3(str='123')
except ValidationError:
    # pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for MyModel
    # str
    #   Input should be None [type=none_required, input_value='123', input_type=str]
    #     For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.7/v/none_required
    ...

# Bug
class M4(BaseModel):
    bytes: Optional[bytes] = None


try:
    m4 = M4(bytes=b'123')

    # pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for M4

    #   Input should be None [type=none_required, input_value=b'123', input_type=bytes]

# OK
class M5(BaseModel):
    bytes: Optional[str] = None

title: Passing data to nested models
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [X] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

# Problem
I need to validate nested models based on the parent model fields. For example, I want to choose a single value from all list-like fields (`field2` and `field3` in this case) based on the ending of `name`. Each field can be integer-like string or list-like string.
```python
data = {
    "name": "item_2",
    "some_fields": {
        "field1": "1",
        "field2": "2 13 5",
        "field3": "4 6 1",
    }
}
```
I came up with 2 solutions, but each of them has its drawbacks
## Solution 1
The most obvious solution is to use `field_validator` and `ValidationInfo` data for `some_fields`
```python
class SomeFields(BaseModel):
    # big list of optional fields:
    field1: int | None = None
    field2: int | None = None
    field3: int | None = None


class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    some_fields: SomeFields

    @field_validator("some_fields", mode='before')
    def choose_single_value(cls, fields: dict, info: ValidationInfo) -> dict:
        """Choose single value from space separated list based on item name"""
        name = info.data.get("name")
        index_from_name = int(name[-1])
        for k, v in fields.items():
            if " " in v:
                fields[k] = v.split()[index_from_name]
        return fields


validated = Item.model_validate(data)
# > name='item_2' some_fields=SomeFields(field1=1, field2=5, field3=1)
```
But this solution have some performance drawbacks. We use loops both for preparing data (fields_validator mode=before) and for internal pydantic validation. In case of hundreds optional fields inside of `some_fields` it can be noticeable. Besides that, I expect the values of the nested model to be validated in the nested model, looks more "clean" to me
## Solution 2
Better idea IMO is to use `field_validator` for all nested fields and somehow pass `name` to nested model. I achieved it via `info.context.update` in parent model:
```python
class SomeFields(BaseModel):
    # big list of optional fields:
    field1: int | None = None
    field2: int | None = None
    field3: int | None = None

    @field_validator("*", mode="before")
    def choose_single_value(cls, value: str, info: ValidationInfo):
        name = info.context.get("name")
        index_from_name = int(name[-1])
        if " " in value:
            value = value.split()[index_from_name]
        return value


class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    some_fields: SomeFields

    @field_validator("name", mode='after')
    def add_context(cls, v: str, info: ValidationInfo):
        info.context.update({"name": v})
        return v


validated = Item.model_validate(data, context={})
# > name='item_2' some_fields=SomeFields(field1=1, field2=5, field3=1)
```
The problem in this case is the need to initialize context property via `model_validate`, which is inconvenient and sometimes limiting
# Request
1. This is a common validation use case, so there should be some documentation about best ways to validate nested models based on parent data
2. Would be nice to have some way to pass data/context to nested models (via Field, _parent.data, etc). I'm not familiar with the implementation of the library, so I don't know what's possible to achieve. At least I want ConfigDict for default context initialization (`init_context=true`) instead of passing it explicitly in `model_validate` for every model creation.

Maybe I'm missing something and there are better ways to solve my problem.


### Affected Components

- [ ] [Compatibility between releases](https://docs.pydantic.dev/changelog/)
- [X] [Data validation/parsing](https://docs.pydantic.dev/concepts/models/#basic-model-usage)
- [ ] [Data serialization](https://docs.pydantic.dev/conc

title: Pydantic2 fails to parse timedelta strings with days separated by spaces
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Per the datetimes docs page https://docs.pydantic.dev/2.0/usage/types/datetime/, pydantic will accept a string with the following format as a time:

`[-][DD ][HH:MM]SS[.ffffff]`

When using the string `7 00:00:00` which parsed properly as `timedelta(days=7)` in pydantic v1, the field fails to validate:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/home/ubuntu/.local/lib/python3.8/site-packages/pydantic/type_adapter.py", line 256, in validate_python
    return self.validator.validate_python(__object, strict=strict, from_attributes=from_attributes, context=context)
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for timedelta
  Input should be a valid timedelta, "day" identifier in duration not correctly formatted [type=time_delta_parsing, input_value='7 00:00:00', input_type=str]
    For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.6/v/time_delta_parsing
```

It works when appending literal `D` to the day value, and including (or not) a space between the day and the HH:MM:SS string, but it is not evident from the docs that this would be required (I discovered it just by chance).


### Example Code

```Python
from datetime import timedelta
from pydantic import TypeAdapter

# Raises ValidationError
TypeAdapter(timedelta).validate_python("7 00:00:00")

# Returns timedelta(days=7)
TypeAdapter(timedelta).validate_python("7D00:00:00")
TypeAdapter(timedelta).validate_python("7D 00:00:00")
```

title: Datetime validation works incorrectly after Pydantic 2.6 with range parametrized APIs in FastAPI
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

We are using FastAPI with various APIs using datetime ranges in URL path parameters. After trying 2.6 we get large amount of test failures due to Pydantic 2.6 incorrectly allowing dates in datetime range URL params. Now suddenly this is allowed: `some/path/2024-01-01/2024-01-04`. Previously it was blocked as path params are datetime validated. Now the dates magically coerce incorrectly to midnights where range suddenly gets to `[2024-01-01T00:00:00, 2024-01-04T00:00:00]`. But obviously this is unexpected and incorrect as the range-end is at midnight.

How do we block this bad behaviour in all our APIs (in context of range usage) with Pydantic 2.6? This seems to be no FastAPI issue as only change we did was trying out Pydantic 2.6.

### Example Code

```Python
async def test_pydantic_breakage():
    @dataclass
    class SharedTimeRangeParams:
        start_time: datetime = Path(..., description="Query timerange start UTC date-time", examples=["2017-07-21T17:32:28Z"])
        end_time: datetime = Path(..., description="Query timerange end UTC date-time", examples=["2017-07-21T17:32:28Z"])

    app = FastAPI()

    @app.get("/some/path/{start_time}/{end_time}")
    async def handler(time_range: SharedTimeRangeParams = Depends()):
        return {"start": time_range.start_time, "end": time_range.end_time}

    client = TestClient(app)
    # Ok
    res = await client.get("/some/path/2024-01-01T00:00:00Z/2024-01-02T23:59:59.999Z")
    assert res.json() == {"start": "2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00", "end": "2024-01-02T23:59:59.999000+00:00"}

    # Broken in 2.6
    res = await client.get("/some/path/2024-01-01/2024-01-02")
    # In 2.6 end is at midnight which doesn't make sense for API usage in the range param
    # assert res.json() == {"start": "2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00", "end": "2024-01-02T00:00:00+00:00"}

    # This doesn't work in 2.6 anymore
    assert "Input should be a valid datetime" in res.json()["detail"][0]["msg"]
```

title: Alias system doesn't cover basic use case of renaming an `internal` field from `external` usage
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

This is somewhere in-between a feature request and a bug report, but judging from the systematic analysis below, it feels like something isn't quite right with the alias system.

Consider the most basic use case of renaming a field. The goals are:

- Within Python code the field should be named e.g. `internal` consistently. This includes field access `my_instance.internal` and the class constructor `MyModel(internal=42)`. Type checkers like mypy/pyright should consider `internal` as the correct identifier in all Python code.
- To the outside the field should be called e.g. `"external"`. This includes all the usages of `model_validate` + `model_validate_json` in validation direction and `model_dump` + `model_dump_json` in serialization direction.

This feels like a very fundamental use case, because it makes sense that a name is decoupled in code from its external form in the payload -- but consistent within the two worlds.

From my systematic assessment it looks like neither `alias="..."`, `serialization_alias="..."`, `validation_alias="..."` nor combinations with `populate_by_name` seem to cover this use case. The following demo code actually constructs all either possible combinations of using

- only `alias="external"`
- only `serialization_alias="external"`
- only `alias="external"`
- both `serialization_alias="external"` and `validation_alias="external"`

and combines them further with both variations of `populate_by_name` enabled and disabled. In none of the the 8 variations the above goals seems to be achievable. The output of the snippet is:

title: using validate_call on a function before calling the function
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [X] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Hey all, first thanks for the great library.

I just came across the validate_call feature which is very useful. I was wondering if we could even go one step further and allow to validate the argument to a function **before** calling it. In my case I want to validate some configuration that contains kwargs for a function. This function is call in the middle of my code, but I would like to validate it that the parameter are good early in my code.

small example:
```python

class HeavyObjectConfig(BaseModel):
   ...



heavy_object = {"heavy": ...}
func_call_args:  {"func_call": ...}

heavy_object_config = HeavyObjectConfig(**heavy_object)

heavy_object  = load_heavy_object(heavy_object_config) # take half a hour

call(**func_call_args) # where call is function wrap into a `validate_call`
```

In this example I would be able to catch problem when calling the function, but only after waiting half an hour of loading my object. Whereas if I could create a validator object out of the function call, I could call it before loading my object and be sure that everything will be fine when calling the function.


Additionally we could even turn function signature into BaseModel that I could use into another nested BaseModel.

A solution right now is to  create BaseModel that copy the function signature, but this is done manually so it take time and is error prone.

Do you think this is something that pydantic could support ? Codewise it should be fairly easy to do, happy to contribute as well

title: Inconsistent JSON serialization of None keys ("None" instead of "null")
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

During migration from v1 to v2 we discovered a change of behavior when serializing `None` keys in a dictionary to JSON.

Since non-string keys are invalid in JSON, both V1 and Python's `json.dumps` opt to serialize `None` to `"null"`. This makes a lot of sense considering that JS's deserialization does translate `"null"` to a regular null (`JSON.parse('{"null": 123}') # => {null: 123}`).
In V2, they are serialized as `"None"`.

This is an undocumented change that can cause unexpected problems due to the deviation from the old behavior that aligns with Python's and JS's implementations.

This may be a breaking change for implementations where Pydantic is used alongside JS, which is often the case with FastAPI../

### Example Code

```Python
class MyModel(BaseModel):
    a: dict[Optional[str], int]

m = MyModel(a={None: 123})

# V1
print(m.json()) # {"a": {"null": 123}}

# V2
print(m.model_dump_json()) # {"a":{"None":123}}
```

title: Generic Type Inference on parse
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

There is a surprising behavior when type-inference mixes with pydantic's handling of generics.
It works beautifully until it starts interacting with "type inference."  In the case below, the generic-argument to `ItemBound` can be inferred from the constructor arguments, so it is surprising when the serialized model returns no values.  Whatever the explanation for the behavior, it's surprising that by removing a bound on a type-variable things "start to work."

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import TypeVar, Generic
from pydantic import BaseModel

TBound = TypeVar("TBound", bound=BaseModel)
TNoBound = TypeVar("TNoBound")

class IntValue(BaseModel):
    value: int

class ItemBound(BaseModel, Generic[TBound]):
    item: TBound

class ItemNoBound(BaseModel, Generic[TNoBound]):
    item: TNoBound

item_bound_inferred = ItemBound(item=IntValue(value=3))
item_bound_explicit = ItemBound[IntValue](item=IntValue(value=3))
item_no_bound_inferred = ItemNoBound(item=IntValue(value=3))
item_no_bound_explicit = ItemNoBound[IntValue](item=IntValue(value=3))

print(f"# inferred and bound: {str(item_bound_inferred.model_dump()):26} {item_bound_inferred.__class__.__name__} -> {item_bound_inferred.item.__class__.__name__}")
print(f"# explicit and bound: {str(item_bound_explicit.model_dump()):26} {item_bound_explicit.__class__.__name__} -> {item_bound_explicit.item.__class__.__name__}")
print(f"# inferred, no bound: {str(item_no_bound_inferred.model_dump()):26} {item_no_bound_inferred.__class__.__name__} -> {item_no_bound_inferred.item.__class__.__name__}")
print(f"# inferred, no bound: {str(item_no_bound_explicit.model_dump()):26} {item_no_bound_explicit.__class__.__name__} -> {item_no_bound_explicit.item.__class__.__name__}")

# inferred and bound: {'item': {}}               ItemBound -> IntValue
# explicit and bound: {'item': {'value': 3}}     ItemBound[IntValue] -> IntValue
# inferred, no bound: {'item': {'value': 3}}     ItemNoBound -> IntValue
# inferred, no bound: {'item': {'value': 3}}     ItemNoBound[IntValue] -> IntValue
```

### Description

There seems to be a breaking change in v2.4. When I run `mypy` against my code I see:

```
error: Variable "pydantic.FieldValidationInfo" is not valid as a type  [valid-type]
note: See https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/common_issues.html#variables-vs-type-aliases
