note: See https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/common_issues.html#variables-vs-type-aliases
error: pydantic.FieldValidationInfo? has no attribute "data"  [attr-defined]
```

This worked in `pydantic==2.3.0` (confirmed with downgrade).

In the [2.3 version of the migration docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev/2.3/migration/#changes-to-validators-allowed-signatures), `FieldValidationInfo` is the recommended way to type the `info` parameter to `field_validator`s. However this has been removed from the [2.4 version of the migration docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev/2.4/migration/#changes-to-validators-allowed-signatures).

In v2.4, I can see this in `pydantic/__init__.py`:

```
# FieldValidationInfo is deprecated, and hidden behind module a `__getattr__`
'FieldValidationInfo': ('pydantic_core', '.core_schema'),
```

but this is missing from v2.3. Is this an intentional breaking change to a minor release? I can't see anything about it in the changelog.

Note: I think this is only broken in the  `pydantic.mypy` plugin, because `FieldValidationInfo` is importable, and it does have the `field_name` and `data` attributes which `mypy` thinks are missing.

Possibly relates to #7617 

Many thanks.

from pydantic import BaseModel, FieldValidationInfo, field_validator


class Model(BaseModel):

        print(info.config.get('title'))
        #> Model

Model(x=1)

title: Partial update of nested model via dump -> copy -> parse doesn't work on v2
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

With v1, doing a partial update of a model instance from another instance could be done via
```py
data = input_model.dict(exclude_unset=True)
updated_model = model.copy(update=data)
```
(this is even a [recommended way in FastAPI docs](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/?h=partial#using-pydantics-exclude_unset-parameter))

There's a caveat though. If those models had nested attributes/values (i.e. sub models),
the resulting `updated_model` will have a `dict` as a value instead of the sub model instance.

To fix/workaround this problem in v1 one could use this trick:
```py
updated_model = updated_model.parse_obj(updated_model)
```

In v2 this trick no longer works.

Is there any way to parse/validate nested values/objects like this?

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel


class SubModel(BaseModel):
    foo: int


class Model(BaseModel):
    bar: str
    sub: SubModel


model = Model(bar="bar", sub={"foo": 0})

# check that foo on sub is 0
assert model.sub.foo == 0


class InputModel(BaseModel):
    sub: SubModel


input_ = InputModel(sub={"foo": 1})

input_data = input_.dict(exclude_unset=True)
updated_m = model.copy(update=input_data)

# now check that foo on sub is 1
# this will raise AttributeError
try:
    assert updated_m.sub.foo == 1
except AttributeError as ex:
    assert str(ex) == "'dict' object has no attribute 'foo'"
else:
    assert False, "were expecting AttributeError"

# trick in v1 to fix this
updated_m = updated_m.parse_obj(updated_m)
assert updated_m.sub.foo == 1
```

With v2, the above code still generates:

```
AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'foo'
```

This is even the case if we get rid of the deprecation warnings:

```diff
--- /tmp/model_update.py	2023-09-10 13:16:14
+++ /tmp/model_update_v2.py	2023-09-10 13:16:24
@@ -22,8 +22,8 @@
 
 input_ = InputModel(sub={"foo": 1})
 
-input_data = input_.dict(exclude_unset=True)
-updated_m = model.copy(update=input_data)
+input_data = input_.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)
+updated_m = model.model_copy(update=input_data)
 
 # now check that foo on sub is 1
 # this will raise AttributeError
@@ -35,5 +35,5 @@
     assert False, "were expecting AttributeError"
 
 # trick in v1 to fix this
-updated_m = updated_m.parse_obj(updated_m)
+updated_m = updated_m.model_validate(updated_m)
 assert updated_m.sub.foo == 1

```

Interestingly, if the `input_data` had invalid data (e.g. `"x"` instead of `1`),
calling `model_validate` would still pass.

title: Performance tips docs page
body:
Page in the docs with tips on using pydantic in the most performant way.

Should start with a big notice saying something like "In most cases pydantic won't be your bottle neck, only follow this if you're sure it's necessary blah blah blah".

1. Use `model_validate_json()` not `model_validate(json.loads(...))` (👀 FastAPI)
2. `TypeAdapter` instantiated once - generally avoid constructing validators and serializers more than necessary
3. `Sequence` vs `list`/`tuple` - `Mapping` vs `dict`
4. Don't do validation when you don't have to - use `Any` to keep the value unchanged
5. generally avoid recording extra information via subclasses of primatives
6. Use tagged union, not union
7. Use `Literal` not `Enum` (not sure how big this effect is)
8. use `TypedDict` over nested models
9. Avoid wrap validators if you really care about performance

Anything else?

title: Refactor documentation
body:
The docs are currently a bit of a mess in terms of their structure.

I think we should restructure the documentation into the following sections:
* **API docs** - which has virtually all the current content - details on how to use it, and some examples
* **Examples** - which is a grab bag of useful examples, a bit like [bootstrap examples](https://getbootstrap.com/docs/4.0/examples/) but just code
* **Concepts** - which will probably be quite small but will cover stuff that doesn’t fit above, e.g. more abstract ideas - this will be more long form and abstract and probably won't get that much coverage attention but good to have
* Existing sections which should remain mostly unchanged:
  * All the pages in the root left menu - "Why use Pydantic", "Help with Pydantic" etc.

  * Settings documentation, currently https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/usage/pydantic_settings/ - I guess this could just go in the same file as the API documentation for `pydantic-settings?

We should work hard to cross link lots.

title: Allow access to strict-mode JSON type coercions after JSON decode
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/get-started/) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Context/Background:
Reported issue: https://github.com/psalvaggio/dynapydantic/issues/33
and the fix I came up with: https://github.com/psalvaggio/dynapydantic/pull/34

To distill the above context to a smaller reproducer:

```python
from pathlib import Path

from pydantic import BaseModel, TypeAdapter, ValidationError

class Model(BaseModel, strict=True):
    file_path: Path

adapter = TypeAdapter(Model)

decoded_json = {
    "file_path": "/tmp/example.txt",
}

# This is the value a field-level validator receives after
# model_validate_json() has decoded the JSON document.
try:
    adapter.validate_python(decoded_json, strict=True)
except ValidationError as exc:
    print("validate_python failed:")
    print(exc)

# Pydantic's JSON validation accepts the same string in strict mode
# and performs the JSON-specific Path coercion.
result = adapter.validate_json(
    '{"file_path": "/tmp/example.txt"}',
    strict=True,
)

print(result)
# Model(file_path=PosixPath('/tmp/example.txt'))
```

Given the constraints I have in my library, it would be desirable to be able to access the available type coercions in strict-mode JSON validation from the TypeAdapter. I could see this taking one of two forms:

1. Allow `strict` on `validate_python` to also take `"json_strict"` or something like that. This is appealing as a non-breaking API change.
2. Allow `validate_json` to take an already decoded object. This seems less desirable.

title: Allow arbitrary core schemas for serialization
body:
As per the TODO in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/13487:

There is currently no way to tell `pydantic-core` "serialize this value using this core schema". `Ser`Schema is:

```python
SerSchema = Union[
    SimpleSerSchema,
    PlainSerializerFunctionSerSchema,
    WrapSerializerFunctionSerSchema,
    FormatSerSchema,
    ToStringSerSchema,
    ModelSerSchema,
]
```

The only member that expresses "use this schema" is `SimpleSerSchema`, and it does not take a schema at all, only a name from a closed literal:

```python
ExpectedSerializationTypes = Literal[
    'none', 'int', 'bool', 'float', 'str', 'bytes', 'bytearray', 'list', 'tuple',
    'set', 'frozenset', 'generator', 'dict', 'datetime', 'date', 'time', 'timedelta',
    'url', 'multi-host-url', 'json', 'uuid', 'any',
]

class SimpleSerSchema(TypedDict, total=False):
    type: Required[ExpectedSerializationTypes]
```

So an arbitrary schema (a model, a dataclass, `list[int]`, a TypedDict, anything constructed by the schema generator) cannot be used directly. Every place in Pydantic that needs it works around the gap the same way: it wraps the schema in a wrap serializer whose function is the identity, purely so the schema can ride along in the `schema` argument.

From `ValidateAs.__get_pydantic_core_schema__()`:

https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/27f95c789b20aa23306e5ce559327db0e9a10a6e/pydantic/functional_validators.py#L911-L917

title: Add Prototype() in the metadata's Annotated of a function attribute for TypeAdapter to use
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/get-started/) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Hi,

My use case is in Fastmcp where i want my tool (python function) to accept incomplete BaseModel (missing fields, no model validation). The idea is to use the filled information as a search query and return to the llm all BaseModel that match. 

Fastmcp uses TypeAdapter for calling the function tool (validate_python) and also for getting the JSON schema (json_schema) that will be sent to the llm.

Consider the following example:

```python
from typing import Annotated, List, Union
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, Prototype # new Prototype class

class Car(BaseModel):
    owner: Annotated[str, Field()]
    color: Annotated[str, Field()]

class Bus(BaseModel):
    company: Annotated[str, Field()]
    color: Annotated[str, Field()]

vehicules: List[Union[Car, Bus]] = []

def get_vehicules(
    vehicule: Annotated[Union[Car, Bus], Prototype()],
):
    results = [found for found in vehicules if found.__class__ == vehicule._class__]
    for field in vehicule.__class__.model_fields:
        if hasattr(vehicule, field):
            for result in results:
                if getattr(result, field) != getattr(vehicule, field):  # will need a correct __eq__ for BaseModel fields
                    results.remove(result)
    return results

# adapter that knows that the vehicule attribute is a prototype because of Protoype()
adapter = TypeAdapter(get_vehicules)
# send the JSON Schema of get_vehicules to the llm, saying that Car and Bus BaseModel have all their required model fields accepting null values if their current type does not already accept null.
# Then if a field is required in the model, it is still required in the JSON Schema but the llm can put the field to null (this is for pydantic to differentiate a bus from a car)
adapter.json_schema()
# get the blue cars
search_result = adapter.validate_python({"vehicule": {"owner": None, "color": "blue"}})  # None is null in JSON
# get the blue buses
search_result = adapter.validate_python({"vehicule": {"company": None, "color": "blue"}})
``` 

Note: you may need first to support dictionary (python/json) for fields of type BaseModel in model_construct. Today it only supports BaseModel instance. See issue 8084.

class MySQLDialect_mariadbconnector_async(MySQLDialect_mariadbconnector):
    """

        engine = create_async_engine(

title: BaseModel-like API for top-level discriminated unions
body:
### Description

This is related to #10409, especially the later comments asking whether `TypeAdapter` can behave more like a `BaseModel`.

Using the docs example:

```py
from typing import Annotated, Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, RootModel, TypeAdapter


class Cat(BaseModel):
    pet_type: Literal["cat"]
    meows: int


class Dog(BaseModel):
    pet_type: Literal["dog"]
    barks: float


class Lizard(BaseModel):
    pet_type: Literal["reptile", "lizard"]
    scales: bool


type Pet = Annotated[
    Cat | Dog | Lizard,
    Field(discriminator="pet_type"),
]
```

For a nested field, the documented pattern works well:

```py
class Model(BaseModel):
    pet: Pet
```

But for a flat top-level object, the available options all have tradeoffs:

```py
pet = TypeAdapter(Pet).validate_python({"pet_type": "cat", "meows": 3})
pet.pet_type  # works
pet.model_dump()  # works
```

But `TypeAdapter` itself is not model-like:

```py
TypeAdapter(Pet).model_validate(...)  # not available
```

`RootModel` gives a model-like API, but wraps the actual object under `.root`:

```py
class PetModel(RootModel[Pet]):
    pass

pet = PetModel.model_validate({"pet_type": "cat", "meows": 3})
pet.root.pet_type  # works
pet.pet_type       # does not
```

Is there, or should there be, a Pydantic-native way to define a top-level discriminated union that:

- preserves the flat input/output shape
- selects the correct concrete model using the discriminator
- is constructible/validatable like a `BaseModel`
- exposes the selected model's fields directly, without `.root`

In other words, something with the ergonomics of `TypeAdapter(Pet).validate_python(...)`, but with a first-class model-style API.

This feature request is for a single, global flag added to the configuration:

- If it is True: serialisation / de-serialisation uses the enum name, and generated schemas contain a list of enum names.

title: Ability to pass context to __get_pydantic_core_schema__ and __get_pydantic_json_schema__
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

I maintain the following library: https://github.com/psalvaggio/dynapydantic https://psalvaggio.github.io/dynapydantic/latest/

The general idea of the library is to offer polymorphic validation to mirror the polymorphic serialization that has been added to pydantic. Essentially, classes keep track of their children via `__pydantic_init_subclass__`, register them, the create unions to serve as field annotations.

Initially, I made this work with a custom annotation around the base class, but I have come up with a way to make the following syntax work:

```python
import dynapydantic
import pydantic

class Base(
    dynapydantic.SubclassTrackingModel,
    union_mode="smart",
    implicit_polymorphic=True,
):
    pass

class A(Base, extra="forbid"):
    a: int

class B(Base, extra="forbid"):
    other: Base

B(other={"other": {"other": {"a": 2}}}) # B(other=B(other=B(other=A(a=2))))
```

This requires overriding `__get_pydantic_core_schema__` and `__get_pydantic_json_schema__`, which works fine in the typical usage.

However, I'm running into issues with inheritance. Consider the following simple tree:

```python
Base <- Mid <- Leaf
```
If I put `Base` (let's pretend it is abstract) into my model, I'd want the field to accept `Mid` and `Leaf`, which are concrete. If I put `Mid` in there however, I'd want it to accept `Mid` or `Leaf`. Same thing if `Base` was not abstract and would be acceptable. This leads to two paths's to `__get_pydantic_core_schema__`:

1. If I use the type directly as a field annotation. Here I want to make the validator that validates the union.
2. If I am making a TypeAdapter from a base class's schema. Here I want the schema that would have been produced had I not overridden `__get_pydantic_core_schema__`.

However, I haven't been able to find a way to make this work. I've tried hacking around with patching the method away or using `contextvars`, but I think pydantic is caching the schema after the first call, which makes sense.

I think having a mechanism to pass context to `__get_pydantic_core_schema__` would allow me to make this all work, assuming the context itself was folded into the caching key.

Would this be a viable feature to add?

title: `model_copy(deep=True, update=...)` unnecessarily deepcopies fields that will be replaced by `update`
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

When calling `model_copy(deep=True, update={...})`, the current implementation deepcopies the **entire** model first, then applies the `update` dict afterwards:

```python
# pydantic/main.py
def model_copy(self, *, update=None, deep=False):
    copied = self.__deepcopy__() if deep else self.__copy__()  # full deepcopy first
    if update:
        ...
        copied.__dict__.update(update)  # then overwrite
    return copied
```

This means fields specified in `update` are deepcopied and then immediately discarded. This causes two problems:

1. **Wasteful performance**: fields that will be replaced are deepcopied for nothing.
2. **Fails on non-copyable fields**: if a field contains an object that cannot be deepcopied (e.g., native C extensions, file handles, GPU tensors), `model_copy` raises an error — even though the caller explicitly intends to replace that field via `update`.

### Example Code

```python
import mujoco
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class PhysicsEngine:
    """Wraps a native MuJoCo simulation (not deepcopy-safe)."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.model = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string("<mujoco/>")
        self.data = mujoco.MjData(self.model)


class AppConfig(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(arbitrary_types_allowed=True)

    name: str = "default"
    engine: PhysicsEngine = None


config = AppConfig(engine=PhysicsEngine())

# This FAILS even though we are replacing `engine`:
copy = config.model_copy(
    deep=True,
    update={"engine": None},  # explicitly replacing the non-copyable field
)
# ValueError: negative dimensions are not allowed
# (from deepcopy trying to copy the MuJoCo native structs)
```

### Proposed Solution

**Option A (minimal):** Add a parameter (e.g., `update_before_copy: bool = False`) to control the order of operations:

```python
def model_copy(self, *, update=None, deep=False, update_before_copy=False):
    if update_before_copy and update:
        # Apply update on a shallow copy first, then deepcopy
        shallow = self.__copy__()
        # apply update to shallow copy
        ...
        copied = shallow.__deepcopy__() if deep else shallow
    else:
        # Current behavior (backward compatible)
        copied = self.__deepcopy__() if deep else self.__copy__()
        if update:
            ...
    return copied
```

**Option B (better default):** When `deep=True` and `update` is provided, skip deepcopy for fields present in `update`. This is both more efficient and avoids the unnecessary failure:

```python
def model_copy(self, *, update=None, deep=False):
    if deep and update:
        # Shallow copy first, apply update, then deepcopy only the remaining fields
        copied = self.__copy__()
        copied.__dict__.update(update)
        for key, value in copied.__dict__.items():
            if key not in update:
                copied.__dict__[key] = deepcopy(value)
    elif deep:
        copied = self.__deepcopy__()
    else:
        copied = self.__copy__()
        if update:
            copied.__dict__.update(update)
    return copied
```

title: Support for x-enum-varnames (Enum member names) in JSON Schema Generator
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Hi! Thanks for the great library!

I need support for the `x-enum-varnames` OpenAPI 3 extension field in the JSON Schema Generator and was curious to see whether there is interests in adding support directly to pydantic, rather than simply creating a custom generator.
I have implemented a [PR](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/13004), and would love to commit it if there is interest.

### Context

`x-enum-varnames` maintains the key(name) of any enum value that defines it in the form `name = 'value'`.
  The default behavior is to use the value as both the key and value.
  This is a frequently supported extension field in OpenAPI 3 and is used by many code generators to allow generating bot Python and Typescript enums in the following form:

```python
class Fruit(Enum):
    apple = 'Apple'
    grape = 'Grape'
``` 
```typescript
export enum Fruit {
    apple = "Apple",
    grape = "Grape"
}
``` 

Without this extension we lose this extra information, and a 1:1 recreation of the original code is impossible:
```python
class Fruit(Enum):
    Apple = 'Apple'
    Grape = 'Grape'
``` 

### Proof Of Concept
In my PR I have added a new option 

**`use_x_enum_varnames`**: `bool`
Default: `False`
```
Whether the generated json-schema/OpenAPI 3 enums should have the `x-enum-varnames` extension populated.
This maintains the key of any enum value that defines it in the form `key = 'value'`.
The default behavior is to use the value as both the key and value.
This is a frequently supported extension field in OpenAPI 3.
```

### Example

```python
from enum import Enum

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class SomeEnum(Enum):
    FOO = 'foo'
    BAR = 'bar'
    BAZ = 'baz'

class DefaultModel(BaseModel):
    value: SomeEnum

DefaultModel.model_json_schema()['$defs']['SomeEnum']
# "SomeEnum": {
#     "enum": ["foo", "bar", "baz"],
#     "title": "SomeEnum",
#     "type": "string"
# }

class VarnamesModel(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(use_x_enum_varnames=True)
    value: SomeEnum

VarnamesModel.model_json_schema()['$defs']['SomeEnum']
# {
#     'enum': ['foo', 'bar', 'baz'],
#     'title': 'SomeEnum',
#     'type': 'string',
#     'x-enum-varnames': ['FOO', 'BAR', 'BAZ'],
# }
```

title: `BaseModel.model_zip()` - construct a list of models from column-oriented data
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

A common pattern when working with Pydantic models is constructing a list of instances from parallel sequences - essentially a column-to-row transpose:

```python
orders = [
    Order(customer=c, product=p, quantity=q)
    for c, p, q in zip(customers, products, quantities, strict=True)
]
```

This comes up frequently in data processing pipelines, ETL code, and API layers where intermediate results are naturally columnar (one list per field) but the final output is a list of validated models.

**Proposed API**

A classmethod on `BaseModel`:

```python
orders = Order.model_zip(customer=customers, product=products, quantity=quantities)
```

Equivalent to the comprehension above, but:

- Validates that all sequences have the same length (raises on mismatch)
- Each row is validated through the normal model constructor

Of course, the name doesn't have to be `model_zip` :)

**Why this belongs in Pydantic**

`model_zip` would be a natural batched counterpart to normal model construction. Pydantic already provides field-aware tooling around model instantiation, including mypy plugin support and editor support in  e.g., VS Code. A built-in `BaseModel.model_zip(...)` would extend that experience to the common case where data is organized by field rather than by row.

Pydantic is also the right layer for this because it already owns the model’s field definitions and runtime validation semantics. While users can validate `list[MyModel]`, they still need to manually transpose columnar inputs first. `model_zip` would fill that gap with a small, explicit API for a common pattern.

**Alternatives considered**

- **Keep the comprehension**: Works, is type-safe (the IDE sees the constructor call), but verbose and repetitive when the pattern recurs across many call sites. This repetition is what brought me to write this request.
- **`TypeAdapter`**: Validates data against a type but has no columnar construction API.
- **`Unpack[TypedDict]`** (PEP 692): Could type specific kwargs, but AFAIK requires a separate TypedDict per model -- defeats the purpose of a generic utility. Unless I'm missing something?

title: Add `exclude_extra` option to `model_dump` and `model_dump_json`
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

If a pydantic base model allows extra fields, they get included in `model_dump` by default, e.g.
```python
class A(BaseModel, extra="allow"):
    a: int

a = A(a=1, b="test")
print(a)  # A(a=1, b='test')
print(a.model_dump())  # {'a': 1, 'b': 'test'}
```
There are cases where we might want to exclude the extra fields from being dumped. The requested feature being something like
```python
print(a.model_dump(exclude_extra=True))  # {'a': 1}
```
`exclude_extra` would be `False` by default preserving the current behaviour.

Technically, this can be done today by doing something like
```python
a_dict = a.model_dump()
for k in a.model_extra:
    a_dict.pop(k)
```
But this is cumbersome, especially if doing `model_dump_json` since you have to deserialize, remove extra fields and then reserialize the dict, which defeats the point of calling `model_dump_json`. Having the option to exclude the extra fields to begin with would be nice.

title: Stdlib dataclass custom docstrings suppressed from JSON schema description
body:
source https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/pull/4138#discussion_r2818450381

### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Pydantic suppresses `__doc__` from stdlib dataclasses in JSON schema generation to avoid auto-generated signature docstrings (e.g. `'Foo(x: int = 1)'`) leaking as `description`. However, the suppression doesn't distinguish between auto-generated and custom docstrings — explicit docstrings are also dropped.

This is inconsistent with Pydantic dataclasses, which DO get their custom docstrings included.

The suppression is in `GenerateJsonSchema.dataclass_schema` (`pydantic/json_schema.py`):

```python
if is_stdlib_dataclass(cls):
    # vanilla dataclass; don't use cls.__doc__ as it will contain the class signature by default
    description = None
```

And similarly in `_update_class_schema`:

```python
docstring = None if cls is BaseModel or dataclasses.is_dataclass(cls) else cls.__doc__
```

Python makes it straightforward to distinguish auto-generated from custom docstrings — the auto-generated ones start with `f'{cls.__name__}('`.

This became more visible after #11822 fixed `is_stdlib_dataclass` (previously `is_builtin_dataclass`), which had a bug where dataclasses with `KW_ONLY` sentinel annotations were not recognized as stdlib dataclasses and accidentally got their docstrings preserved.

### Example Code

```python
# /// script
# requires-python = '>=3.10'
# dependencies = [
#     'pydantic>=2.12',
# ]
# ///
import dataclasses

import pydantic
import pydantic.dataclasses
from pydantic import TypeAdapter


@dataclasses.dataclass
class StdlibNoDoc:
    x: int = 1


@dataclasses.dataclass
class StdlibWithDoc:
    """A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."""

    x: int = 1


@pydantic.dataclasses.dataclass
class PydanticWithDoc:
    """A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."""

    x: int = 1


print(f'pydantic=={pydantic.__version__}')
print()

for cls in [StdlibNoDoc, StdlibWithDoc, PydanticWithDoc]:
    schema = TypeAdapter(cls).json_schema()
    desc = schema.get('description')
    print(f'{cls.__name__}:')
    print(f'  __doc__     = {cls.__doc__!r}')
    print(f'  description = {desc!r}')
    print()
```

### Output

```
pydantic==2.12.5

StdlibNoDoc:
  __doc__     = 'StdlibNoDoc(x: int = 1)'
  description = None

StdlibWithDoc:
  __doc__     = "A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."
  description = None

PydanticWithDoc:
  __doc__     = "A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."
  description = "A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."
```

**Expected**: `StdlibWithDoc` should also have `description` set since it has an explicit custom docstring.

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```
pydantic version: 2.12.5
python version: 3.13.3
platform: macOS
```

title: Extract type arguments used to specialize generic models at run-time
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

I've been working on porting a Pydantic V1 [application](https://salsa.debian.org/freexian-team/debusine) to V2, and in the process found myself needing to import from `pydantic._internal._generics`.  Neither my reviewer nor I can think of a better way to do things at the moment, but we agreed it would make sense to file an issue upstream.

A number of parts of our database schema are structured with a category field and some JSON data fields; the category field selects the schema used to parse the JSON data fields.  For example, we have several different kinds of "artifact", each of which has its own schema for "artifact data".  The code to handle each artifact of course wants to work with a validated Pydantic model instance rather than the raw JSON data, but we wanted to keep things reasonably DRY by not repeating the code needed to construct the model in lots of different places.

I invented a pattern that we've found to work well across our application.  When ported to Pydantic V2, it looks something like this (reduced):

```python
import abc
import enum
from types import GenericAlias
from typing import Any, ClassVar, Generic, TypeVar, cast

import pydantic
from pydantic._internal._generics import get_args, get_origin


# The return type is really typing._GenericAlias, but that's private.
def _get_specialization(cls: type, base: type) -> Any:
    """
    Inspect a class for its specialization of a generic base class.

    A class may specialize a generic base class in various ways: for
    example, it might supply specific values for some of the relevant type
    variables, or it might itself be generic and rely on being specialized
    by its own subclasses, or both.  To help us introspect such classes,
    this returns the specialization of `base` by `cls` in the form of a
    :py:class:`typing._GenericAlias`.

    :raises AssertionError: if `cls` specializes `base` in different ways by
      means of multiple inheritance.
    """
    specializations: set[GenericAlias] = set()
    if hasattr(cls, "__pydantic_generic_metadata__"):
        orig_bases = [get_origin(cls)[get_args(cls)]]
    else:
        orig_bases = getattr(cls, "__orig_bases__", [])
    for cls_base in orig_bases:
        origin = get_origin(cls_base)
        if origin == base:
            specializations.add(cls_base)
        elif origin is not None and issubclass(origin, base):
            specializations.add(
                _get_specialization(origin, base)[get_args(cls_base)]
            )
    if len(specializations) != 1:
        raise AssertionError(
            f"{cls.__qualname__} must specialize {base.__qualname__} with "
            f"exactly one consistent list of type arguments "
            f"(got {specializations})"
        )
    [specialization] = specializations
    return specialization


def extract_generic_type_arguments(
    cls: type, expected_origin: type
) -> tuple[type, ...]:
    """
    Extract type arguments from a generic class.

    This is expected to be called from __init_subclass__ in a generic class
    (i.e. one that has Generic[...] as a base class), and allows extracting
    the specializing type arguments so that they can be used as factories.
    """
    args = get_args(_get_specialization(cls, expected_origin))
    assert isinstance(args, tuple)
    return args

    SOURCE_PACKAGE = "debian:source-package"

class DebianSourcePackage(ArtifactData):
    name: str
    version: str
    dsc_fields: dict[str, Any]


AD = TypeVar("AD", bound=ArtifactData)

title: Improve logic around `ImportString` validation when the `ImportError` originates from another source
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When something else (and not the `ImportString` import path) produces an `ImportError`, `ImportString`'s error handling catches the exception and assumes it has been produced by the user-provided import path. 

This results in a misleading and confusing exception message. 

### Example Code

```py

from pydantic.types import ImportString

adapter: TypeAdapter[type] = TypeAdapter(ImportString)

import_path = "my_module.MyClass"

print("Attempting to validate import path:", import_path)
print()

# What Pydantic reports:
print("=== Pydantic ImportString error ===")
try:
    adapter.validate_python(import_path)
except Exception as e:
    print(f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}")

print()

# What the actual error is:
print("=== Actual ImportError ===")
try:
    import my_module
except ImportError as e:

```

### Description

I would like to propose adding a built in `Port` type, similar in spirit to existing network types.

When handling configuration, network ports can be very common. It would be ideal if, when parsing such configuration, ports could be represented in a type safe and semantically meaningful way.

Ports have a clear meaning, and while it can be argued that ports are simply integers with a defined range, this semantic information is currently lost in most model definitions.

Currently, a way to solve the issue with having a typesafe `Port` could be the following:

```python
Port = Annotated[int, Field(ge=0, le=65535)]

class SomeConfig(BaseModel):
    port: Port
```

While the above example works, it leads to each project needing to define its own type. I believe implementing `Port` can provide a more centralized and reusable definition. It could also raise the intuition that a port also needs to be validated and not simply be taken as is, and applications would be able to fail at an earlier stage.

title: Premature warning about Python 3.14 in pydantic.v1
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When a module is imported `from pydantic.v1` and a user is running Python 3.14, they'll get a warning: "Core Pydantic V1 functionality isn't compatible with Python 3.14 or greater."

On the surface, the logic here is sound: if the user is importing something from `pydantic.v1` they must be about to use that thing, so let's warn them that it's not going to work.

But there are packages that import classes from V1 just to _check_ if the end user is using V1. For example, [LangChain in this file](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/blob/master/libs/core/langchain_core/utils/pydantic.py).

In these cases, the warning is confusing and sends developers down a rabbit hole of trying to work out "who's trying to use Pydantic V1?" and if they don't know Python intimately, they might think that different packages are using different versions of Pydantic at the same time and they're clashing, all rather unpleasant, considering that nothing's actually wrong!

I see three possible futures:
1. Python 3.14 users in this situation get warnings, they can ignore them (warning fatigue, not great)
2. All packages that do this "import from `pydantic.v1` to check usage" pattern fix their code to check in some way that doesn't involve importing from `pydantic.v1` (probably not going to happen)
3. Pydantic refines the logic to only show this warning when it looks like something is actually going to break (e.g. triggered in the constructors of classes)

The current logic is going to be helpful to a shrinking number of users, and rather annoying for a growing number of users.

Relevant PR: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/12263

title: [Request] Built-in validation of lists and dicts of BaseModels (e.g. via RootModel children)
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Suppose I have a simple model:

```python

from pydantic import BaseModel

Foo(BaseModel):
    bar: str
```
I might have an external data source that will sometimes return a `Foo`, but other times it might return a `list[Foo]` or `dict[something, Foo]`. How do you validate this? A naive approach might be `[Foo.model_validate(foo) for foo in response]`. This often works, but what if `response` is not a `list`? Or it's a `dict` instead (in which case you're inadvertently making a list of the keys).

It's very convenient to have pydantic handle all of these edge cases for you. One way is another `BaseModel` child with a `list[Foo]` attribute. Another way is by using `RootModel`. This is nice because it also lets you take advantage of `Protocol` to automatically call `model_validate` on arbitraily-typed responses from your external data sources. If for some reason, though, you need the post-validation object to be used directly (e.g. 3rd party library), then having to carry around the `.root` makes this break.

What we end up doing in our libraries is something like this:

```python
_V = TypeVar("_V", bound=BaseModel)

class ListModel(RootModel[list[_V]]):
    def append(self, value: _V):
        self.root.append(value)

    def extend(self, values: Iterable[_V]) -> None:
        self.root.extend(values)

    def insert(self, index: SupportsIndex, value: _V) -> None:
        self.root.insert(index, value)

    # And so on; whatever other methods we need.
```

You can do something similar with `dict`.

It would be great if something to handle these types of scenarios were built into pydantic to enable something like these:
```python
from pydantic import ListModel

class ListOfFoo(ListModel[Foo]):
    pass

ListOfFoo.model_validate(data)

Baz = ListModel[Foo]

baz = Baz.model_validate(response)
baz[0]
baz.pop()
# etc
```

I'm not convinced our approach is the best one, but I haven't come across anything else that's wildly better. Another possibility we considered was something like:
```
from pydantic import ListOf

result: list[Foo] = ListOf(Foo).model_validate(response)
```
It's nice to return the list directly rather than have it wrapped in a subclass, but there were too many edge cases to worry about.

title: Allow raising custom model validation exceptions
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

It can sometimes be useful to treat validation errors coming the same model differently, based on the place in the code, where the validation was attempted.

One particular use case for this is a web application, which puts data fetched from a database into a model instance. `ValidationError` raised here should be considered a server-side error and treated differently from failing to validate a request body (which is a client-side error).

One way to differentiate validation failures is to allow setting an exception class or instance to be re-raised from a `ValidationError`, i.e.:

```python
class Model(BaseModel):
    # `model_config` can contain an optional exception class to be used by default for `Model`
    model_config = ConfigDict(custom_validation_exception=SomeException)
```

```python
def model_validate(
    ...
    # An override for the specific `model_validate` call, which has the priority
    # over `model_config` exception, if set, and could be provided with `ValidationError`
    # to disable re-raising
    custom_validation_exception: Exception | type[Exception] | None = None
):
    ...
    # `CustomExceptionContextManager` catches `ValidationError` and re-raises `exc` from it,
    # if `exc` is not resolved to None or `ValidationError`
    exc = custom_validation_exception or cls.model_config.get("custom_validation_exception")
    with CustomExceptionContextManager(exc):
        return cls.__pydantic_validator__.validate_python(
        ...
        )
```

Another potential option is to restrict both `custom_validation_exception` values to `ValidationError` and its subclasses and use them directly in pydantic-core (although I can't properly assess the possibility & the amount of work required to do so).

It's certainly possible to add similar exception handling on the side of a library user, however a Pydantic implementation of this feature -- at least for the `model_validate` & `model_validate_json` methods -- seems to be less verbose and should not introduce any breaking changes.

body:

### Description

Currently,even if a type can be converted, the type-checker/linter will show an error
```python
class Number(BaseModel):
   value: int

   @model_validator(mode="before")
   @classmethod
   def _from_string(cls, value):
        if isinstance(value, dict):
            return value
        return {"value": value}

   def _from_string(cls, value):
        if isinstance(value, dict):

        return {"value": value}

title: Allow documenting custom type aliases via typing_extensions.Doc
Preserve `NamedTuple` class during validation
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

This is what I'm observing:

```Python
import pydantic
from typing import NamedTuple


class A(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class B(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    a_or_b: A | B


c = C(a_or_b=B(x=1))
print(c)

# expected: a_or_b=B(x=1)
# prints: a_or_b=A(x=1)
```

This short-circuits on type arguments in the union in order in the `smart` mode of unions (`left_to_right` I assume makes no difference, the problem lies in exactness).
If we reverse it, the output will show `B` because `B` was first that structurally matched.

It works this way in strict mode too.
This resembles `left_to_right` more than `smart` mode of the union schema.

Conceptually, Pydantic looks for ways to match namedtuple as a structural type, whereas the nominal bit was missed.

This applies to old-fashion named tuples as well:
```py
from collections import namedtuple

import pydantic

A = namedtuple('A', 'x')
B = namedtuple('B', 'x')

class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    a_or_b: A | B

c = C(a_or_b=B(x=1))
print(c)  # a_or_b=A(x=1)
```

We would want to convert between uniform namedtuples in non-strict mode -- sure:

```py
import pydantic
from typing import NamedTuple


class A(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class B(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    only_a: A


c = C(only_a=B(x=1))
print(c)  # only_a=A(x=1)
```

but I'm not so sure we want the union schema to miss the nominal type of the input. If we can preserve the original type, my instinct is that we'd want to keep it. Esp. since we don't observe this behavior with dataclasses (namedtuples are of quite different nature, though).

The current behavior can be interpreted as a feature, not a bug -- feel free to relabel this as a feature request if you do think that's true.

## In short

I'm proposing a feature to, in validation, validate every namedtuple input against its targeted namedtuple class (so, `return_schema` -- seems like `return_schema` isn't used by namedtuple schemas yet) **before** proceeding with the call validator logic and deconstructing it as a collection of arguments and trying a call to the namedtuple constructor. It would be based on a new `idempotent` flag in `CallValidator` -- if a function call is idempotent, the validation should start from the return validator -- if that doesn't pass, only then try to call. As a result, nominal types wouldn't be swapped in unions of namedtuples in smart union mode.

Do you guys think this is worth adding to pydantic, or too much hassle for an edge case?
Thanks!

PS One more thing. This relies on the assumption that instance checks guarantees type safety of the object's state.

If the namedtuple instance contains unsound data, its internals wouldn't be re-validated and fixed up in place as it happens right now. In this sense, the change could be breaking. 

The same that would happen here already happens for dataclasses in Pydantic:

```py
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic import BaseModel


@dataclass
class Foo:
    x: int


malformed = Foo(x="1")

class Model(BaseModel):
    foo: Foo

print(Model(foo=malformed))
```

If someone has an unsure instance of a namedtuple, they would need to re-validate it through type adapter, perhaps.
Or just use models directly on raw data -- for 99.999% of people this won't happen.

title: Docstrings leaking into JSON Schema descriptions impact agentic production systems
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

In Pydantic v2, a model’s class docstring automatically becomes the "description" field in the generated JSON Schema. This is convenient for documentation, but it implicitly makes comments part of the runtime contract because many runtimes (especially LLM and agent frameworks) now consume those schemas directly to decide behavior.

A harmless docstring edit can change tool selection or behavior in production.

This coupling is amplified because LLM platforms explicitly encourage Pydantic for structured output/tool schemas (ie [OpenAI](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/structured-outputs) and I believe PydanticAI has same risk although I haven't had the time to experiment there yet).

Developers don’t expect docstrings to affect runtime behaviour.
The software folklore tale [The Inner JSON Effect](https://thedailywtf.com/articles/the-inner-json-effect) illustrates how comments bleeding into contracts can become a subtle foot-gun.


LLM agents often read schema "description"s to decide which tool/model to use; a teammate “polishing” a docstring can alter production outcomes.
On top of that, docstrings are frequently edited without the same review rigor as public contracts.


### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Foo(BaseModel):
    """An example base model"""
    pass


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(Foo.model_json_schema())

# > {'description': 'An example base model', 'properties': {}, 'title': 'Foo', 'type': 'object'}
```

title: Add utility function to convert Pydantic model fields to dictionary representation for API documentation
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description


## Summary
Add a utility function that converts Pydantic model fields to a human-readable dictionary representation, particularly useful for generating API documentation and Swagger/OpenAPI schemas.

## Motivation
When building APIs with Pydantic models, developers often need to programmatically generate documentation that shows the expected structure of request/response bodies. Currently, there's no built-in way to convert a Pydantic model field structure into a clean, readable dictionary format that can be easily used for:

- Auto-generating API documentation
- Creating Swagger/OpenAPI schema descriptions
- Providing clear examples in API responses
- Debugging and development tools

## Proposed Solution
A new utility function `pydantic_model_to_dict()` that would:

1. **Handle nested models**: Recursively process Pydantic models within models
2. **Support primitive types**: Convert basic Python types (int, str, float, etc.) to readable names
3. **Handle Optional types**: Properly format `Union[Type, None]` as `Optional[Type]`
4. **Support Union types**: Format multiple type unions as `[type1, type2]`
5. **Handle collections**: Format `List` and `Dict` types with their contained types
6. **Support Enums**: Display enum values as readable options

## Example Usage
```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import Optional, List, Dict
from enum import Enum

class Status(Enum):
    ACTIVE = "active"
    INACTIVE = "inactive"

class User(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: Optional[int]
    status: Status
    tags: List[str]
    metadata: Dict[str, str]

# Would output something like:
# {
#   "name": "str",
#   "age": "Optional[int]", 
#   "status": "<active, inactive>",
#   "tags": "List[str]",
#   "metadata": "Dict[str, str]"
# }
```

## Benefits
- Improves developer experience when building APIs
- Reduces boilerplate code for documentation generation
- Provides consistent formatting across different projects
- Enhances debugging capabilities for complex model structures

## Implementation Considerations
- Should handle all current Pydantic field types
- Needs proper error handling for unsupported types
- Should maintain performance for large, deeply nested models
- Could be placed in `pydantic.utils` or similar module

Would this be a valuable addition to the Pydantic library? I've already done an implementation in local.

body:

### Description

I suggest changing the type of pattern in `fields.py` generally to `str | re.Pattern[str] | None` from the current `str | typing.Pattern[str] | None`. `typing.Pattern` is deprecated with replacement `re.Pattern[str]` since Python 3.9, which is the minimum version Pydantic V2 supports, so `re.Pattern[str]` certainly is available. This change should not change the behaviour of the library.

Other occurrences of `typing.Pattern` in the code might also be considered for change, but some might relate to user uses of it (I am not familiar enough with the code to judge this) and thus change the behaviour of the library, therefore I do not suggest a general change.

I did not find this functionnality, si here is what I did with transformers.Seq2SeqTrainingArguments.__init__ as an example function

import inspect

from pydantic import create_model, BaseModel
from pydantic.config import ConfigDict
from transformers import Seq2SeqTrainingArguments


def config_from_function(func) -> type[BaseModel]:
    """Create pydantic model from function signature."""
    sig = inspect.signature(func)
    fields = {}
    for name, param in sig.parameters.items():
        if name == "self":
            continue
        annotation = (
            param.annotation
            if param.annotation != inspect.Parameter.empty
            else (
                str if param.default == inspect.Parameter.empty else type(param.default)
            )
        )
        default = param.default if param.default != inspect.Parameter.empty else ...
        fields[name] = (annotation, default)
    config = ConfigDict(arbitrary_types_allowed=True, strict=False)

    model = create_model(
        f"{func.__name__.capitalize()}Model", **fields, __config__=config
    )
    return model

title: Stabilize `MISSING` sentinel feature
body:
This will depend on the fate of [PEP 661](https://peps.python.org/pep-0661/).

Things to consider:
- [x] We probably should push down constraints, e.g. `int | MISSING = Field(gt=1)` should be equivalent to `Annotated[int, Gt(1)] | MISSING`. What about `int | None | MISSING`? https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/12908
- [x] When validation fails for  `<typ> | MISSING`, we shouldn't mention `MISSING` as an allowed value in the validation error. This may require some changes in the core schema logic (currently this is a union, which shouldn't have special knowledge about `MISSING` being one of the union members, so we probably need something similar to the `'nullable'` schema). https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/13779
- Related to previous point, should `MISSING` actually be allowed as a value? Is there a use case where explicitly allowing `MISSING` (only possible from Python, not JSON) makes sense? Shouldn't it be some kind of implementation detail? Final decision: we decided it should be allowed, as it would otherwise contradict static type checkers, and we can see how it can be useful (e.g. setting a field to `MISSING` after validation to exclude it).

    ```python
    class Model(BaseModel):
        a: int | MISSING = MISSING

    model = Model(a=MISSING)  # This currently works

    # As per the type checking rules for sentinels, this is a static type checker error:
    class Model(BaseModel):
        a: int = MISSING

    # .. if this was possible, then the sentinel is only relevant as a default value. Conceptually, it means
    # *not* having a default value is a logical error?
    class Model(BaseModel):
        a1: int
        # equivalent to?:
        a2: int | MISSING
    ```

title: Proposal: Subclass-tracking dynamic base models
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

I have a proof-of-concept for how such a feature might work here:

https://github.com/psalvaggio/dynapydantic#

Problem I am looking to solve:

Getting inheritance to work through a serialization/validation roundtrip is difficult and often requires the use of discriminated unions. The problem gets worse if potential subclasses can be spread across multiple Python modules, or even worse, multiple Python packages.

Toy example: https://github.com/psalvaggio/dynapydantic/tree/main/tests/example

Package `my-animal`:

Defines a base class Animal, which wants this behavior of being able to be serialized and reprised as any subclass (demonstrated in the `parse` command on the CLI). It inherits from `DynamicBaseModel` and passes a discriminator field of its choosing:
```python
class Animal(abc.ABC, dynapydantic.DynamicBaseModel, discriminator_field="type"):
    @abc.abstractmethod
    def speak(self) -> None:
        pass
```
Subclasses can be defined elsewhere in `my-animal` just fine.

Package `dog-plugin`: https://github.com/psalvaggio/dynapydantic/tree/main/tests/example/dog-plugin

Another person comes along and wants to add into this architecture:
```python
import typing as ty

import dynapydantic
import my_animal

class Dog(my_animal.Animal):
    type: ty.Literal["Dog"] = "Dog"
    bark_volume: int

    def speak(self) -> None:
        print("woof" if self.bark_volume < 50 else "WOOF")

@dynapydantic.hookimpl
def register_models() -> list[my_animal.Animal]:
    return [Dog]
```

Then in a virtual environment with both `my-animal` and `dog-plugin` installed:
```
> my-animal parse '{"type": "Dog", "bark_volume": 60}'
type='Dog' bark_volume=60
WOOF
> my-animal parse '{"type": "Cat", "name": "Kitty"}'
type='Cat' name='Kitty'
Kitty says meow
> my-animal list
{'Cat': <class 'my_animal.cat.Cat'>, 'Dog': <class 'dog_plugin.Dog'>}
```

Why should this go into pydantic as opposed to just being a separate library?

This feels like a very common use case and would probably benefit a large number of users. While it is not necessary for using inheritance with pydantic, I do find myself re-implementing boilerplate like this often.

If this was implemented as a `BaseModel` subclass as I did in the POC, this would be a pure opt-in feature and would pose no backwards-compatibility concerns.

The `pluggy` dependency is probably a sticking point in here. It is a pretty common one for anyone that is using pytest already, which is going to be a lot of users. An alternative solution probably exists using `importlib`, or the `pluggy` part of this could be made into an opt-in feature.

title: `Secret` is unnecessarily invariant, can be made covariant
body:
I noticed that the generic `Secret` type is unnecessarily invariant, which means that valid usages like this fail to type check:

```py
from pydantic import Secret

def takes_secret(scalar_secret: Secret[str | int | float | bool]):
    ...

def secret_usage() -> None:
    secret: Secret[str] = Secret('my secret')
    takes_secret(secret)
```

Currently that last line does not type check, because the invariance prevents to accept e.g. a `Secret[str]` where a `Secret[str | ...]` is expected. Note that this restriction is unnecessary: `Secret` is an immutable type, both practically and conceptually. It's a typical covariant use case and there is no need to enforce invariance. The type can be made covariant similarly to how e.g. `Sequence` or `Mapping` are covariant thanks to immutability.

I can prepare a small PR for fixing it.

title: Document exceptions handled by `PlainValidator`'s callback (and handle `TypeError` as `ValueError` ?)
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Considering current `PlainValidator`'s docstring:

https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/88c75cd5adbfbfea4ff1aceb597c93f238db8dcb/pydantic/functional_validators.py#L166-L191

1. The exceptions `func` should raise to indication a validation error is not documented
2. The example doesn't give an example of invalid validation
3. Passing another type than `str` or `int` will cause a `TypeError` to be raised instead of the excepted `ValidationError`

Point 1 & 2 means the user relies on implicit information to understand how `PlainValidator` works (typically since `int()` raises `ValuError` and `TypeError` it can be assumed both types are handled).

Point 3 is especially annoying since it means an application can crash if extra care hasn't been taken, for instance if a malicious user sends `{"a": {}}`, then `Model.model_validate_json('{"a": {}}', strict=True)` will raise a `TypeError` :/

To give a bit more context: I've encountered this issue while using Pydantic with FastAPI for validating a JSON REST API, in this case it's a big footgun, especially since the `PlainValidator` in the example uses a `lambda` to define the validation function: a lambda looks small&slick, but doesn't allow catching exception, which further give the impression handling `TypeError` is not needed...


Regarding what could be done to improve this, I would say the best would be to:
- Handle `TypeError`  along with `ValueError` (typically providing a different error message depending on which one is caught)
- Document that `func` only allow `ValueError`&`TypeError` exceptions
- Improve the example to also try to validation with an invalid type (or an invalid value, but it would require more changes since the example relies on integer addition which has no invalid value...)

Of course the drawback of this is it would break compatibility (but I would say it is for the better ^^), the alternative would be:
- Document that `func` only allow `ValueError` exception
- Update the example to have a try/except on `TypeError` (re-raising a `ValueError`) and also try to validate with an invalid type

title: Support for a no_data_value that bypasses built-in validators like ge and le
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

**Background**
I have a Pydantic model with numeric fields that use constraints such as ge and le for validation.
In my data, I use a special sentinel value (e.g., -9999) to represent "no data" or missing data in my scientific data

**Problem**

- If I declare a field like Field(..., ge=0, le=100, metadata={"no_data_value": -9999}) and pass the sentinel value -9999, the validation fails as expected.
- I tried using a @field_validator with mode='before' to transform the sentinel into a valid value, but the built-in validators (ge, le) are still applied after that, causing a validation error.
- An after validator never runs because validation stops on the first error.
- I applied a @field_validator with mode='before' to transform the sentinel into a value within the valid range, allowing the built-in validators (ge, le) to pass. Then, I use an after validator to transform the value back to the original sentinel no_data_value. However, this workaround is dangerous


**Request**

I would like a native feature in Pydantic that allows specifying a no_data_value sentinel for a field that:

- When encountered, skips all built-in validators like ge, le, min_length, max_length, etc.
- Allows having strict validation on normal values and silently accept the sentinel as a valid special case.

**Example**

```python
class Model(BaseModel):
    temperature: float = Field(..., ge=0, le=100, no_data_value=-9999)

# This should pass validation:
Model(temperature=-9999)
```



### Affected Components

title: Properly expose FieldInfo
body:
### Initial Checks

### Description

When inspecting models dynamically, I mainly use the `model_fields` attribute to get the `FieldInfo` for each field and do something with it. Sometimes it is necessary to import `FieldInfo` to annotate a function receiving it.

In Pycharm, imports are checked for their public visibility. This includes checking the `__all__` attribute, if one exists. When importing `from pydantic.fields import FieldInfo`, I get a warning stating that `'FieldInfo' is not declared in __all__ `, which is true. All the other public members (no leading underscores) in this module are declared. Simply adding `'FieldInfo'` resolves the warning.

Also, would it make sense to also expose `FieldInfo` from the root pydantic package? It is the only public member in `pydantic.fields` that is not importable from there.

I am not sure how to reproduce this with tools other than pycharm. All the usual tools (ruff, pyright, mypy, pylint, pyflakes, flake8) do not seem to care about this, or I am missing some opt-in rule configuration.

### Example Code

from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic.fields import FieldInfo  # warning: 'FieldInfo' is not declared in __all__

def main() -> None:

title: Model Validator in Field level
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

I have tried to figure whether there exists a way to achieve the following mechanism directly on the field level, however, I do not seem to be able to find such an approach.


Current working approach:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic.functional_validators import model_validator


def merge(values: dict):
    return ", ".join(values.keys())


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    merged: str

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    def merge(cls, data: dict):
        data["merged"] = merge(data)
        return data


model = MyModel.model_validate({"A": 1, "B": 2, "C": 3})
print(model.model_dump_json(indent=2))
```


Desired working approach:

```python
class DummyNestedModel(BaseModel):
    merged: Annotated[int, BeforeValidator(merge)] = Field(validation_alias=None)
```

Obviously the `validation_alias=None` approach won't work, however, somehow I would still expect that it could e.g. pass the full object (i.e. the incoming object in `model_validate()`) for validation, such that I am not forced to select only one field, when I e.g. want to merge two fields into one and make a derived field.

I am aware that the desired functionality for the outcome already exists, and that this is more of a subjective view on how to handle it differently. The reason for preferring the second approach would be in the cases when you have models with e.g. +100 fields, where you have a lot of custom validators, it might be easier to have the overview of validations directly next to the field, rather than at the bottom of the model with a lot of logic going on in the `model_validator` wrapper.

title: Add ability to exclude a type from serialization.
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Use-case:
I have a 'missing' sentinel value. When the field is set to this sentinel I want it to be excluded from the model serialization.

This discussion is relevant: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/discussions/9943#discussioncomment-10131374 

This is different from `Field(exclude=true)` as that's on a per field level. I could do it on a per model basis by having a custom wrap serializer, but that requires that every model that uses the sentinel must also support this custom serializer. 

I'd propose adding a `core_schema.exclude_ser_schema()` and an `ExcludeSerialization` annotation.
```python
@classmethod
def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(cls, source_type: Any, _: GetCoreSchemaHandler) -> core_schema.CoreSchema:
    return core_schema.is_instance_schema(
        cls=source_type,
        serialization=core_schema.exclude_ser_schema(),
    )
```

And 
```python
class MyModel(BaseModel):
    nullable_field: str | None | ExcludeSerialization[MissingSentinel] = MISSING
```


Calling `model_dump(exclude_unset=True)` comes very close in the desired behaviour but I'd like to keep other defaults. 
For example, I want this:
```python
class MyModel(BaseModel):
    nullable_field: str | None | ExcludeSerialization[MissingSentinel] = MISSING
    some_number: int = 100

MyModel().model_dump() == {"some_number": 100}
```

---
Full example with feature requests as comments:
```python
from typing import Any

from pydantic import GetCoreSchemaHandler, GetJsonSchemaHandler
from pydantic.json_schema import SkipJsonSchema
from pydantic_core import core_schema


class _MissingSentinel:
    """Use this to have different behaviour between
        Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/discussions/9943#discussioncomment-10131374
    """
    _instance = None

    def __new__(cls):
        if not cls._instance:
            cls._instance = super().__new__(cls)
        return cls._instance

    def __repr__(self):
        return "<MISSING>"

    @classmethod
    def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(cls, source_type: Any, _: GetCoreSchemaHandler) -> core_schema.CoreSchema:
        return core_schema.is_instance_schema(
            cls=source_type,
            # Feature request: 
            # serialization=core_schema.exclude_ser_schema(),
            serialization=core_schema.to_string_ser_schema(),
        )

    @classmethod
    def __get_pydantic_json_schema__(cls, core_schema: core_schema.CoreSchema, handler: GetJsonSchemaHandler):
        return {}

# Feature Request: 
# MissingSentinel = SkipJsonSchema[ExcludeSerialization[_MissingSentinel]]
MissingSentinel = SkipJsonSchema[_MissingSentinel]
MISSING = _MissingSentinel()


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    nullable_field: str | None | MissingSentinel = MISSING
```

class Something(BaseModel):
     someField: int = 0  #  description: Some description text
```

replaces 
```
class Something(BaseModel):
     someField: int = Field(default=0, description="Some description text")

or 

```
class Something(BaseModel):
    """ A Something.

    fields:
    * someField:  Some description text
    """

* Potential conflicts with mypy, ruff and other "comments readers"

title: 🚀 Feature Request:  Support `NotRequired` Field Semantics in Pydantic Models
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description


## 🚀 Feature Request:  Support `NotRequired` Field Semantics in Pydantic Models

### Background

In many real-world API contracts, some request fields are:

- Optional to include (i.e., the client may omit them entirely),
- But if provided, **must be a valid non-null value**,
- And **`null` is not a valid input** (and often not semantically meaningful),
- Meanwhile, default values might exist on either client or server side,
- And sometimes you *want* to keep Pydantic’s default values for internal logic, while only omitting them from serialized outputs under certain rules.

Currently, Pydantic does not provide a clean, expressive way to represent this intent.

---

### 🔍 Motivation

Consider the following server-side API contract:

```json
POST /predict
{
  "model": "gpt-4",
  "temperature": 0.7   // optional, but if provided must be a float between 0 and 1
}
```

The rules are:

1. The `temperature` field is optional — if omitted, the server uses its own default.
2. If provided, it **must be a float**, and **must not be `null`**.
3. The client should be able to omit it without sending a dummy value like `0.0`.

---

### 🧪 Existing Workarounds (and Their Issues)

#### 1. `temperature: float | None = None`

```python
class Request(BaseModel):
    model: str
    temperature: float | None = None
```

**Problem:**
- This accepts `"temperature": null`, which violates the API contract.
- `null` is not a valid temperature — but this model would allow it.

---

#### 2. Use `.model_dump(exclude_none=True)`

**Problem:**
- Some fields may legitimately use `None` as a value (e.g. `description: str | None`).
- `exclude_none=True` will strip *all* `None`s, even if some are semantically meaningful.
- No per-field control over `None` exclusion.

---

#### 3. Use `temperature: float = 0.0` and `.model_dump(exclude_defaults=True)`

```python
class Request(BaseModel):
    model: str
    temperature: float = 0.0
```

**Problem:**
- 0.0 might be a valid and meaningful temperature.
- Can't distinguish between "use server default" vs. "I want zero".
- `exclude_defaults=True` affects all fields, not just `temperature`.

---

#### 4. Use `.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)`

```python
class Request(BaseModel):
    model: str
    temperature: float = 0.7
```

**Problem:**
- Works for `temperature`, but fails for cases where you *want* the defaulted field to be included.

Example:

```python
class FunctionTool(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["function"] = "function"
    function: dict
```

- `type` should always be included in the output (required by server).
- But `exclude_unset=True` will remove it unless explicitly set by the user.
- Again, too broad — no per-field control.

---

#### 5. Use `TypedDict + TypeAdapter` (which supports `NotRequired`)

```python
from typing import TypedDict, NotRequired
from pydantic import TypeAdapter

class RequestDict(TypedDict, total=False):
    model: str
    temperature: NotRequired[float]

TypeAdapter(RequestDict).validate_python({"model": "gpt-4"})
```

**Problem:**
- `TypedDict` does not support default values.
- For example:

  ```python
  class FunctionToolDict(TypedDict):
      type: Literal["function"]  # must be manually set every time
      function: dict
  ```

  - There's no way to pre-fill `type = "function"` as a default.
  - Developer must remember to manually set it every time — error-prone and inconvenient.

- `TypedDict` also lacks many useful features from `BaseModel`:
  - Validation logic,
  - Serialization methods (`model_dump`),
  - Field validators, default factories, etc.

In short: `TypedDict` gives you `NotRequired`, but takes away everything else that makes Pydantic useful.

---

### 🧩 What's Missing: `NotRequired`

We need a way to express this common API pattern

title: validate_call is missing a check for the classmethod decorator.
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Validate_call doesn't check whether it is applied to a classmethod when validate_call is not used as a decorator (see Example Code).

This case would be useful to check in order to prevent a developer from applying validate_call to an external package without consideration and encountering strange bugs.

A possible fix could involve making a call in _check_function_type:

```python
def _check_decorator(function: object) -> None:
    """Check if the function is a decorator from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/19227724/check-if-a-function-uses-classmethod."""
    bound_to = getattr(function, '__self__', None)
    if not isinstance(bound_to, type):
        return
    name = function.__name__
    for cls in bound_to.__mro__:
        descriptor = vars(cls).get(name)
        if descriptor is not None and isinstance(descriptor, (classmethod, staticmethod, property)):
            name = type(descriptor).__name__
            raise PydanticUserError(
                f'The `@{name}` decorator should be applied after `@validate_call` (put `@{name}` on top)',
                code=_INVALID_TYPE_ERROR_CODE,
            )
    return
```
I can make a PR if necessary.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import ConfigDict, validate_call


class Parent:
    @classmethod
    def must_not_crash(cls):
        """Check that must_not_crash is called with the child class."""
        assert cls.__name__ == "Child"


class Child(Parent):
    @classmethod
    def must_not_crash(cls):
        """Call super with cls=Child."""
        super().must_not_crash()


# If we want to add validate_call after
Parent.must_not_crash = validate_call(config=ConfigDict(strict=True))(Parent.must_not_crash)
Child.must_not_crash()
```

body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything

### Description

(based on [this](https://docs.pydantic.dev/dev/contributing/#adding-your-library-as-part-of-pydantics-third-party-test-suite))

[Cadwyn](https://github.com/zmievsa/cadwyn) is an API versioning framework based on FastAPI and pydantic. It generates pydantic models and python enums on the fly based on migrations written by the end users of the framework.

For example, the following version change from Cadwyn will make cadwyn generate another version of UserCreateRequest and UserResource while renaming the field `addresses` to `address` and changing its type from `list[str]` to `str`.

```python
class ChangeAddressToList(VersionChange):
    description = (
        "Give user the ability to have multiple addresses at the same time"
    )
    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(UserCreateRequest)
        .field("addresses")
        .had(name="address", type=str),
        schema(UserResource).field("addresses").had(name="address", type=str),
    )
```

Since it uses a ton of internal pydantic interfaces to do this, even minor compatibility issues between pydantic releases can break Cadwyn. Since Cadwyn is used in Airflow from version 3.0, it seems to make sense to include Cadwyn's test suite in pydantic's. Cadwyn uses tox, pytest, and uv, and heavily relies on its CI (where we test 3.9-3.13 on 3 major platforms).

Probably, this problem occurs only with libraries using generic type at runtime, such as Pydantic. I think a solution with the mypy plugin provided by pydantic could be considered.

title: Support for returning multiple annotations from function
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

# Example Problem

Let us consider the example of adding validators for Path types depending on existence, suffixes, ... Let us call that validator PathConstraints, and let us say we wish to use it in the following way.

```python
class Args(BaseModel):
    path: Annotated[Path, PathConstraints(exists=True, suffix=".csv")]
```

We then write the code for PathConstraints. It returns a AfterValidator, all is well. However, I then wish to also modify the json_schema (or simply use more validators). For this, I use a Field with json_schema_extra. This would work well if we did the following:

```python
class Args(BaseModel):
    path: Annotated[Path, PathConstraintsValidator(exists=True, suffix=".csv"), PathConstraintsField(exists=True, suffix=".csv")]
```
However, this is not what we desire and does not scale as we add validators...

# Attempted solution

Simply return the AfterValidator and the Field from the PathConstraints function and use the following (note the *). But this is not correct python.

```python
class Args(BaseModel):
    path: Annotated[Path, *PathConstraints(exists=True, suffix=".csv")]
```
Note that this problem was also encountered [here](https://www.reddit.com/r/learnpython/comments/18z655u/dynamic_annotated_types/) with exactly the same attempt...

# Current pydantic solution ?

I believe I can achieve what I need using __pydantic_core_schema__ and the equivalent json schema function. However, my understanding was that composing basic annotations should be the way to go (most of the time) and that we should not need to use __pydantic_core_schema__ for simple tasks.

# Full example code

```python
def general_path_constraint_checker(p: Path, exists: Union[bool, None], patterns: List[str], type):
    if exists is None: pass
    elif exists:
        if not p.exists():
            raise ValueError(f'Path {p} does not exist')
    elif not exists and p.exists():
        raise ValueError(f'Path {p} exists and should not')

    if type!="any":
        if p.exists():
            if type=="folder" and not p.is_dir():
                raise ValueError(f'Path {p} should be a folder')
            elif type=="file" and p.is_dir():
                raise ValueError(f'Path {p} should be a file. Got a folder')
    if patterns:
        for pat in patterns:
            if re.match(pat, str(p)):
                return p
        raise ValueError(f'Path {p} should match one of the following patterns {patterns}')
    return p

def PathConstraints(exists: Union[bool, None] = None, type: Literal["file", "folder", "any"] = "any",
                    suffix: Union[str, List[str]] =[], patterns: Union[str, List[str]] =[], enforce_pattern: bool=True):
    if isinstance(patterns, str):
         patterns = [patterns]
    if isinstance(suffix, str):
         suffix = [suffix]
    patterns+=[f"^.*{re.escape(s)}$" for s in suffix]
    return (AfterValidator(lambda p: general_path_constraint_checker(p, exists, patterns if enforce_pattern else [], type)), 
            Field(json_schema_extra=lambda d: d.update(dict(pattern="("+ ")|()".join(patterns) + ")"))))
```
