title: Support "default" in generated schema when default_factory is used
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

After reading #1836 I understand that it was decided (#1504) to stop filling the "default" field in the JSON schema generated by models that use `default_factory`, but I think this behavior should be customizable as some of us might face cases where the absence of the "default" value is problematic.

My use-case is similar to #1520: I am developing an API using FastAPI and I will use the generated JSON schema to automatically render a form so non-technical users can interact with my endpoints on a website. One of my fields is the current date (not datetime), which needs a `default_factory` to provide a default value:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from datetime import datetime

class Parameters(BaseModel):
    today: str = Field(default_factory=lambda: datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))
```

In my case I want the default value to be included in the JSON schema for the following reasons:

- Unlike a `datetime` field and because of my user's usage patterns, there is no chance that the value will change between checking the schema and calling the endpoint (which I understand was a source of concern from [this comment](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/1836#issuecomment-674552982)).
- It might be confusing for some developers (like me) that instantiating the model without arguments, like `Parameters()`, works fine, while the JSON schema indicates that 'today' is a mandatory field. This supports the idea that the current behavior may not be universally intuitive, so a customizable behavior would be beneficial.
- I chose to automate the form creation using the JSON schema to avoid maintaining the form's rendering logic per endpoint, but if there is a chance that people ask me "how do I fill the 'X' field?", it's going to become a source of inconvenience that I can't automate.

I adapted what is proposed in [this hack](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/1836#issuecomment-674584438) like this:

```python
class BaseModelDefaultFactory(BaseModel):
    @classmethod
    def model_json_schema(cls):
        schema = super().model_json_schema()
        for fld_n, fld_v in cls.model_fields.items():
            if fld_v.default_factory is not None:
                print(fld_n)
                schema['properties'][fld_n]['default'] = fld_v.default_factory()
        return schema

class Parameters(BaseModelDefaultFactory):
    today: str = Field(default_factory=lambda: datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))
```

But I would prefer that it becomes something that we can configure by field or by model, instead of a hack that I must remember and maintain with each Pydantic update (which I already had to do, so it's already a problem).

### Description

Currently `use_attribute_docstrings=True` doesn't work in interactive sessions such as when using a jupyter notebook. This is quite sad since it makes code look a lot cleaner in my opinion.

I'm currently monkeypatching the required functionality in a utility library. Would it be possible to add this functionality to pydantic? If desired I can send a PR.

Here's the ugly monkeypatchy code i'm currently using:
```python
if is_ipython():
  from pydantic._internal import _docs_extraction

  _extract_source_from_frame = _docs_extraction._extract_source_from_frame

  def extract_source_from_ipython(cls):
    from IPython import get_ipython
    from IPython.core.magics.code import extract_symbols

    shell = get_ipython()  # type: ignore
    cells = shell.user_ns["In"]
    cell = cells[-1]
    blocks, not_found = extract_symbols(cell, cls.__name__)
    if len(blocks) >= 1:
      return blocks[0]
    return None

  def extract_source_from_frame(cls):
    if is_ipython():
      source = extract_source_from_ipython(cls)
      if source is not None:
        return source

    return _extract_source_from_frame(cls)

  _docs_extraction._extract_source_from_frame = extract_source_from_frame
```

Having OnErrorOmit is great when dealing with lists to avoid invalidating the whole model tree if one item in that list is invalid. @model_validator(mode="wrap")

    return handled_data

title: BaseUrl: Provide a property or method to access the encoded URL string.
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

This feature request is the result of hitting a bug in our application and wishing there was a way to prevent it in the future.

## Context

Through the body of this feature request, I use `HttpUrl` as an example, but this feature request likely applies to the whole _BaseUrl hierarchy and possibly other unrelated but similar types.

Imagine a BaseModel looking something like the following:
```python
class MyData(BaseModel):
  my_url: HttpUrl | None
```

And an API like the following:
```python
def store_my_url(my_url: str | None) -> None: ...
```

The important part is that the API of `store_my_url` is very inflexible, and it aggressively checks the type of its input.

The bug we had was with code like the following: `store_my_url(str(my_data.my_url))` (where `my_data: MyData`). Unfortunately, this is almost right, but no tooling(1) will help you identify that you are going to convert `None` into `"None"` which is entirely unintended.

(1) The way we have mypy configured doesn't seem to catch this, and I think we have it on a super strict mode.

## Feature Request / Proposal

It would be nice if there was a property or method like:
```python
@property
def encoded(self) -> str:  # This needs a better name.
  return str(self)
```

This would allow the buggy call to be written as: `store_my_url(my_data.my_url.encoded)` which would have instantly failed type checking and avoided the translation error. This would also make changing the `my_url` field of MyData from `HttpUrl` to `HttpUrl | None` safer as static analysis tooling would be able to identify more places where the type union would need to be updated.

Alternative approaches to solving this problem would also be acceptable as I might have overlooked something. It would be nice if the pattern for converting `HttpUrl | None` to a string representation could be less error prone.

Thanks for your consideration.

title: Convert any type to any type utility (like V1's `parse_obj_as`)
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

`parse_obj_as`, not only got deprecated for the TypeAdapter API in V2, but also removed the functionality of converting BaseModel instances to dicts.
This worked in V1:

```python
class Model(BaseModel):
    x: int


m = Model(x = 5)
d = parse_obj_as(dict, m)
```
but does not in V2.
If we look at the new TypeAdapter API it does not support this functionality either:

```python
TypeAdapter(dict).validate_python(m)
```

This is especially painful in scenarios where you are parsing to dynamic types, and you don't know your type in advance. 
Of course I can do an `if` check to see if the type I am converting to is a dict, and if so do a model_dump, but this seems too verbose and unnecessary for my liking, and also I am not sure what other conversions are supported by `parse_obj_as` but not by `TypeAdapter` APIs, and I don't want to add lots of if checks and essentially implement pydantic all over again myself (for example, `parse_obj_as` not only handled conversion to dict but also but the internal fields of the dicts based on the parameters of the type annotation)
For completeness sake, I suggest to extend the `TypeAdapter` API to allow for any and all conversions supported by Pydantic. The second best option, in case this is viewed as a breaking change or for performance reasons, I would suggest having a separate function that converts any type to any as long as it is supported by Pydantic, similarly to V1's `parse_obj_as`

title: Add Unicode string normalization tests
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing


## Description
I'd like to add a test coverage to test_edge_cases.py for Unicode string normalization. 

### Proposed Test Coverage

- Emoji with zero-width joiners (👨‍👩‍👧‍👦)
- Variation selectors (🏳️‍🌈)
- Skin tone modifiers (👋🏾)
- Combining characters vs precomposed characters (e\u0301 vs é)
- Surrogate pairs (🌍)
- Right-to-left text (سلام)
- Bidirectional text mixing (Hello سلام)
- Korean Hangul decomposition (한)
- Replacement characters (�)
- Zero-width spaces (a\u200Bb)
- Characters with different NFKC/NFKD normalizations (ﬃ)

Proposed Code:
```
def test_unicode_string_normalization():
    class UnicodeModel(BaseModel):
        text: str

    test_cases = {

        "zwj_sequence": "👨‍👩‍👧‍👦",
        "variation_selector": "🏳️‍🌈",
        "skin_modifier": "👋🏾",
        "decomposed_e": "e\u0301",
        "precomposed_e": "é",
        "surrogate_pair": "🌍",

        "rtl_chars": "سلام",  # right to left text
        "mixed_direction": "Hello سلام",  # Mixed RTL and LTR
        "decomposed_hangul": "한",  # Korean character that can be decomposed
        "invalid_sequence": "�",  # Replacement character
        "zero_width": "a\u200Bb",  # Zero-width space
        "different_normalized": "ﬃ",  # Character that differs in NFKC/NFKD
    }

    for case_name, test_str in test_cases.items():
        model = UnicodeModel(text=test_str)
        assert model.text == test_str
        assert len(model.text) == len(test_str) # Checking Length

        json_str = model.model_dump_json()
        decoded = UnicodeModel.model_validate_json(json_str) # Checking if it survived json roundtrip
        assert decoded.text == test_str

        for form in ['NFC', 'NFD', 'NFKC', 'NFKD']:
            normalized = unicodedata.normalize(form, test_str)
            normalized_model = UnicodeModel(text=normalized)
            assert normalized_model.text == normalized

            renormalized = unicodedata.normalize(form, normalized_model.text) # checking if it is stable under normalization
            assert renormalized == normalized
```

body:
### Initial Checks

### Description

According to [documentation](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/standard_library_types/#strings), `LowerCase` and `UpperCase` from `annotated-types` can be used for `str`. However, the string's case remain unchanged. `StringConstraints` works as expected.

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Annotated

from annotated_types import LowerCase, UpperCase
from pydantic import BaseModel, StringConstraints

test_string = "Test String"

# This works
class StrWithStringConstraints(BaseModel):
    upper_case: Annotated[str, StringConstraints(to_upper=True)]
    lower_case: Annotated[str, StringConstraints(to_lower=True)]

print(StrWithStringConstraints(upper_case=test_string, lower_case=test_string))
# output: upper_case='TEST STRING' lower_case='test string'

# This is not working
class StrWithAnnotatedTypes(BaseModel):
    upper_case: Annotated[str, UpperCase]
    lower_case: Annotated[str, LowerCase]

print(StrWithAnnotatedTypes(upper_case=test_string, lower_case=test_string))
# output: upper_case='Test String' lower_case='Test String'
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text
pydantic version: 2.12.3

body:

### Description

**Bug Summary**
When upgrading from Pydantic V1 to Pydantic V2, I encountered a breaking change in model_validator(mode="before").
The same code works perfectly in Pydantic V1, but fails in Pydantic V2 when using model_validate_json(), throwing validation errors due to missing required fields.

**To Reproduce**:
The following is workable v1 codes

```py
import pydantic.v1 as pydantic

class BaseFruit(pydantic.BaseModel):
    name: str

    @pydantic.root_validator(pre=True)
    @classmethod
    def extract_name(cls, data: dict) -> dict:
        assert len(data) == 1
        fruit_name, fruit_attributes = data.popitem()
        return {"name": fruit_name, **fruit_attributes}

class Banana(BaseFruit):
    quantity: int

class NestedFruitOrder(BaseFruit):
    fruits: list["FruitType"]

FruitType = Banana | NestedFruitOrder

class FruitOrder(pydantic.BaseModel):
    fruits: list[FruitType]

FruitOrder.update_forward_refs()
NestedFruitOrder.update_forward_refs()

order_json = '{"fruits": [{"Susan": {"fruits": [{"Nested": {"fruits": [{"Mike": {"quantity": 5}}]}}]}}]}'
order = FruitOrder.parse_raw(order_json)
print(order)

```

title: Nested Validation Errors in Pydantic Models Do Not Propagate Properly
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When creating nested Pydantic models, validation errors from an inner model are not fully propagated to the outer model in certain scenarios, especially when exceptions are re-raised or wrapped during outer model validation. This behavior makes it difficult to debug issues in complex model hierarchies.

In the example below, an InnerModel fails validation because a field does not meet its constraints. However, when this failure occurs during the validation of an OuterModel, the error message only reflects the outer validation failure, potentially obscuring the root cause.



### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError, validator

class InnerModel(BaseModel):
    age: int

    @validator("age")
    def check_age_must_be_positive(cls, value):
        if value <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Age must be positive")
        return value

class OuterModel(BaseModel):
    name: str

    @validator("name")
    def create_inner_model(cls, value):
        # Attempt to create the InnerModel with invalid data
        # Intentionally use a negative age to trigger an error
        InnerModel(age=-1)
        return value

if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        OuterModel(name="Testing")
    except ValidationError as e:
        print("----- Python Exception Output -----")
        print(e)            # Human-readable error
        print("----- JSON Error Output -----")
        print(e.json())     # JSON-formatted error
```

title: PostgresDsn required host - should be optional
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

There is assumption in the code that host is required parameter in PostgresDsn. 

I do think there a number of cases where you won't submit `host` as a parameter as it's not required in many PG drivers. In Google Cloud you can connect in Cloud Run and other environment via unix socket file never going via host network. Example: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/python-docs-samples/blob/main/cloud-sql/postgres/sqlalchemy/connect_unix.py#L36-L37 
```python
        # postgresql+pg8000://<db_user>:<db_pass>@/<db_name>
        #                         ?unix_sock=<INSTANCE_UNIX_SOCKET>/.s.PGSQL.5432
        # Note: Some drivers require the `unix_sock` query parameter to use a different key.
        # For example, 'psycopg2' uses the path set to `host` in order to connect successfully.
        sqlalchemy.engine.url.URL.create(
            drivername="postgresql+pg8000",
            username=db_user,
            password=db_pass,
            database=db_name,
            query={"unix_sock": f"{unix_socket_path}/.s.PGSQL.5432"},
        ),
```
The URI part `postgresql+pg8000://<db_user>:<db_pass>@/<db_name>?unix_sock=<INSTANCE_UNIX_SOCKET>/.s.PGSQL.5432` doesn't have at all host and that is ok for a lot of drivers.

title: 'Url' type casts left around when serializing model to a dictionary
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When serializing a model using URLs back to a dictionary, provided the URLs are properly represented, and validated using any of the network URL types, `Url/AnyUrl/HttpUrl` are explicitly formatted as type casts to the serialized dictionary  (depending on the exact pydantic v2 release)  which makes it hard to deterministically compare data as plain dictionaries in unit tests.
I used the word "deterministically" because prior pydantic  2.10.2 it seems like all URL types where formatted as `Url(<url>)`, but after **2.10.2** where there were adjustments to the URL validation constraints the actual types are honored in the serialized dictionary.
I don't think the type casts should be dumped to a serialized dictionary once a model has been successfully validated, making it completely transparent to the user what the model does/did in the background.

[1] https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/serialization/#modelmodel_dump

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel, AnyUrl
from pprint import pprint


class SubModel(BaseModel):
    bar: AnyUrl
    baz: int = 1


class MainModel(BaseModel):
    foo: Optional[str] = None
    submodels: list[SubModel] = []


m = {
    "foo": "foo",
    "submodels":
        [
            {"bar": "https://example.com"},
            {"bar": "http://www.example.com/path", "baz": 2}
        ],
}

pprint(MainModel.model_validate(m).model_dump())

title: Avoid Models Field Caching
body:
The TestModel does not refresh the `ModelStack` instance whenever the `current_model` changes. As a result, the `TestModel` fails to validate input data correctly when `current_model` is dynamically updated. Specifically, updating `current_model` from `Model` to `Model2` should allow the `TestModel` to use `Model2` for validation, but it continues to reference `Model1`.

**Code to reproduce:**
```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Model1(BaseModel):
    name: str

class Model2(BaseModel):
    numbers: list[int]

current_model = Model1

class ModelStack:
    def __getattr__(self, item):
        return getattr(current_model, item)

class TestModel(BaseModel):
    submodel: ModelStack()

print(TestModel.model_validate({"submodel": {"name": "John Doe"}}))  # Expected: submodel=Model1(name='John Doe')

current_model = Model2
print(TestModel.model_validate({"submodel": {"numbers": [1, 2, 3]}}))  # Expected: submodel=Model2(numbers=[1, 2, 3])
# Actual output:
# 
# pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for TestModel
# submodel.name
#   Field required [type=missing, input_value={'numbers': [1, 2, 3]}, input_type=dict]
#     For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.9/v/missing
```

**Expected Behavior:** The `TestModel` should refresh its `ModelStack` submodel whenever `current_model` is updated. Therefore, after updating `current_model` to `Model2`, `TestModel` should recognize it and validate `{"submodel": {"numbers": [1, 2, 3]}}` correctly.

**Actual Behavior:** The `TestModel` does not refresh the submodel and continues to expect the fields defined in `Model1`, resulting in a validation error.

**Environment (if needed):** 
Python: 3.12.1
Pydantic: 2.9.2

title: `model_dump` dict stays attached to the model's references for custom classes
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

It appears that `model_dump` creates a 'shallow' dump of the model: if one of the model attributes is a custom class containing mutable data, then changing the data in a dump of the model will also change it in the original model.

This feels unexpected as one would expect a 'dump' to be a record (e.g. [core dump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Core_dump), or [database dump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database_dump)) of the model at the time of the dump, and changing that record should not change the original model. I think that either `model_dump` should do 'deep' dumps by default to actually create a dictionary record (and `vars(model)` can be used for `shallow` dumps) or `model_dump` should have an optional `deep` parameter.

A current workaround for this is if you use `model.model_copy(deep=True).model_dump()`, then it works as expected.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class MyClass:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data

class Model(BaseModel, arbitrary_types_allowed=True):
    var: MyClass

m = Model(var=MyClass([1, 2, 3]))
md = m.model_dump()
md['var'].data.pop()

# will give a result of [1, 2], so 3 has been popped from the model as well

  - (I have actually searched GH for similar requests and found #8092 and #9686, which touch upon this.) 
- [X] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Given something like

```python
from typing import Literal, Self

import pydantic


class ServiceConfiguration(pydantic.BaseModel):
    access_key: str | None = None
    endpoint_url: pydantic.HttpUrl | Literal[""] | None = None

    @pydantic.model_validator(mode="after")
    def check_access_key_format(self) -> Self:
        if self.endpoint_url:  # Customized endpoint, do not check format.
            return self
        if self.access_key and not self.access_key.islower():
            raise ValueError(
                "Access key must be lower case. The default service does not tolerate shouting and loud noises.")
        return self


ServiceConfiguration.model_validate({"access_key": "VERYVERYLOUD"})
```

I would like to be able to customize the `loc` for the resulting error to be `'access_key'`, since the error is actually an error in that field, so I can eventually format the `pydantic.ValidationError` to neatly nested JSON with a reference to the actual field that had the issue. 

Some ideas for implementing this:

* Allow setting `field_name` for `model_validator()`s too, and use it for `loc`. Not very dynamic, maybe overloads the `field_name` name too much?
* Read a `loc` or `_pydantic_loc` or similar field off the exception user code raises, use it if available. Simple enough, but also relies on the implicit magic that this is a thing, and creating such an exception is not idiomatic (and may not be possible, if the exception class has e.g. slots):
  ```python
  exc = ValueError("No shouting!")
  exc.loc = ("access_key",)
  raise exc
  ```
* A Pydantic-specific extra error info wrapper exception type?
  ```python
  raise pydantic.ErrorWithContext(ValueError("No shouting!"), loc=("access_key", ))
  ```
  Feels pretty elegant, should be easy to peel off and process in the Rust core code?
* Add `loc` to [`PydanticCustomError`](https://docs.pydantic.dev/dev/api/pydantic_core/#pydantic_core.PydanticCustomError)?

title: Field parsing order is not taken into account for Decimal | str
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

First of all thanks for the amazing library 👏 

I have observed a change in behavior confirmed in 2.9.0 and 2.9.1 compared to 2.8.2.

The type order for Decimal and string in not taken into account. I haven't checked for other types that could behave the same.

# How it used to behave
Having a field annotated `Decimal | str` used to first try to parse to `Decimal` in `2.8.2` then to `str` if the string was not a valid Decimal (e.g. `"5%"`) .

# How it now behaves
In 2.9.0 and 2.9.1, it does not try to parse to Decimal, or at least it always parses to str if the input is a string.

# Changelog
I checked the changelog for 2.9.0 and didn't see anything directly mentioning this change but may have missed something 😕 

There is a tiny change mentionning `Decimal` but it does not look related.
> Move decimal.Decimal validation to _generate_schema.py by @sydney-runkle in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/9977


With a little guidance, I'm up to try and fix this 🙂 

### Example Code

```Python
from decimal import Decimal

from pydantic import BaseModel

class Cover(BaseModel):
  deductible: Decimal | str

cover = Cover.model_validate({"deductible": "0"})

assert isinstance(cover.deductible, Decimal) # evaluates to "False"

title: Potential Issue with model_dump_json in Pydantic: Inconsistent Output Compared to json.dumps
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Hello,

I have encountered a potential issue with the model_dump_json function in Pydantic. Specifically, the JSON string returned by model_dump_json may differ from the output of Python's built-in json.dumps in subtle ways, such as the presence or absence of spaces after colons. This inconsistency can lead to failures in processes that rely on exact string matches, such as MD5 hash-based encryption verification.

Problem Description:

When serializing a Pydantic model to JSON using the model_dump_json method, the resulting JSON string may include or omit spaces after colons differently compared to the json.dumps method. In scenarios where JSON strings must match exactly (e.g., for generating MD5 hashes for encryption verification), these differences can cause validation to fail.

Steps to Reproduce:

Create a Pydantic model.
Serialize the model to JSON using both model_dump_json and json.dumps with specific formatting options.
Compare the resulting JSON strings.


Expected Behavior:

The JSON output from model_dump_json should be consistent with the output from json.dumps(example.dict(), separators=(',', ':')), ensuring no spaces appear after colons, or providing options to control the formatting. This consistency is crucial for processes that depend on exact string matches.

Actual Behavior:

In some cases, the JSON outputs are not identical, particularly regarding spaces after colons. This discrepancy can cause failures in MD5 hash generation and other validation processes that require exact JSON string matches.

Impact:

This inconsistency can cause issues in systems relying on JSON-based encryption or signature verification, where the serialized JSON string must precisely match the string used at the time of signing or encrypting.

    key1: str
    key2: int

example = ExampleModel(key1="value1", key2=123)

pydantic_json = example.model_dump_json()
standard_json = json.dumps(example.model_dump())

### Description



Was expecting dynamic updates made to `model_fields` to carry over to a child class.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic.fields import FieldInfo

class Parent(BaseModel):
    foo: str

# Dynamically add field to Parent model

<details>

<summary>Original issue:</summary>

Was expecting dynamic updates made to `model_fields` to carry over to a child class when using `create_model()` in conjunction with the `__base__` argument. Seems this is not the case. Would have expected `model_fields` to be identical for the base and child class.

from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

If this is a bug rather than a wontfix, i would be happy to PR the behavior with a little guidance on what an acceptable implementation would look like since i know y'all have a high volume of issues <3

also sorry if this is a duplicate, i searched but couldn't find a previous issue



### Example Code

from typing import Any
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, field_validator, ValidationInfo, ValidatorFunctionWrapHandler
from numpydantic import NDArray

class MyModel(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")
    __pydantic_extra__: dict[str, NDArray]

    @field_validator("*", mode="wrap")
    @classmethod
    def cast_fields_wrap(
        cls, val: Any, handler: ValidatorFunctionWrapHandler, info: ValidationInfo

    @field_validator("*", mode="before")

title: unittest.mock.autospec and hastattr()
body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/discussions/2853
Originally posted by **atskae** May 28, 2021 I was mocking out some Pydantic `BaseModel` classes in a `pytest` environment since some of the model's fields were objects from an external package. I learned that if I `autospec` a `BaseModel` *class* (not object), then `hasattr()` is always `False`. This is not the case for normal Python classes: ``` >>> from pydantic import BaseModel >>> class Cat: ... name = None ... >>> class PydanticCat(BaseModel): ... name: str ... >>> cat = create_autospec(Cat) >>> hasattr(cat, 'name') True >>> pydantic_cat = create_autospec(PydanticCat) >>> hasattr(pydantic_cat, 'name') False ``` If I pass in an object `pydantic_cat = create_autospec(PydanticCat(name='meowth'))`, then `hasattr()` works as expected. I was just curious if this design was intentional and whether it is bad practice to `autospec` a Pydantic `BaseModel` class in this way, or if it even makes sense. Thanks!

title: Validation error: 'str' instances not allowed as a Sequence value
body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

The validate_call decorator from Pydantic raises a validation error when a string is passed as a Sequence. According to the Python documentation, a string is a sequence type, but Pydantic's validation does not currently allow 'str' instances to be considered valid for a Sequence.

It happens with ```from collections.abc import Sequence``` and ```from typing import Sequence```.

from typing import Annotated, TypeVar

from pydantic import Field, validate_call

T = TypeVar('T')


@validate_call
def random_choice(sequence: Annotated[Sequence[T], Field(min_length=1)]) -> T:
    return SystemRandom().choice(seq=sequence)


print(isinstance('string', Sequence))  # >>> True

title: 2.8.0 unexpectedly change `create_model()`arg `__model_name` to `model_name`
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Hi!

Not sure if it is a bug or an intended change, but I could not find a mention of it in the release notes, so I'm reporting it anyway.

So essentially, we have some dynamic model generation running, looking like this:
```
def inject_default_from_instance(instance_w_defaults: BaseModel) -> Type[BaseModel]:
    model_w_defaults = create_model(
        __model_name=instance_w_defaults.__repr_name__() + "WithDefaults",
        __base__=type(instance_w_defaults),
        **{
            k: (
                instance_w_defaults.model_fields[k].annotation,
                FieldInfo.merge_field_infos(
                    instance_w_defaults.model_fields[k],
                    default=getattr(instance_w_defaults, k)
                )
            )
            for k in instance_w_defaults.model_fields.keys()
        }
    )
    return model_w_defaults
```

It's a bit hacky and is used to overcome limitations in a different framework, so it may not be the best example of pydantic usage.

Also (our bad, yeah) we have pydantic version set up as "pydantic>=2,<3", so today one of the pipelines picked up the new 2.8.0 version and failed during the test with
TypeError: create_model() missing 1 required positional argument: 'model_name'
from the above-mentioned snippet.

After some digging, I found a [change](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/9479/files#diff-8708af8d26c26644976866f974e0b810b0940ede43ff487e457057d5a1f07999L1446) causing an error in the snippet. Looking at the description, I'm not perfectly sure if the change of the argument name was intended or not.
Probably, if the change is intended, it should be mentioned in the release notes, since it is technically a compatibility change of the public API.

Right now I'll fix the pydantic version more strictly to 2.7, but still would like to know if the change is intended, so I should change the create_model() call accordingly.

title: Pydantic calls model_validator in wrong place
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

The PatientGet model has a decorator that translates some fields from a nested class to the main class. There is also a SuccessSignIn class that takes DoctorGet or PatientGet as input. And the expected behaviour is that when passing DoctorGet, it will not try to call the validator of the PatientGet model. 

### Example Code

```Python
from dataclasses import dataclass

import pydantic


class Base(pydantic.BaseModel):
    model_config = pydantic.ConfigDict(from_attributes=True, extra='forbid')


class PatientGet(Base):
    id: int
    first_name: str | None = pydantic.Field(None, min_length=0, max_length=128)
    middle_name: str | None = pydantic.Field(None, min_length=0, max_length=128)
    last_name: str | None = pydantic.Field(None, min_length=0, max_length=128)

    @pydantic.model_validator(mode='before')
    @classmethod
    def personal_info_to_object(cls, values):
        values.first_name = values.personal_info.first_name
        values.middle_name = values.personal_info.middle_name
        values.last_name = values.personal_info.last_name
        return values


class DoctorGet(Base):
    id: int
    first_name: str | None = pydantic.Field(None)
    last_name: str | None = pydantic.Field(None)


class SuccessSignIn(Base):
    user: PatientGet | DoctorGet
    user_type: str
    access_token: str
    refresh_token: str
    token_type: str


@dataclass
class PersonalInfoOrm:
    id: int
    first_name: str
    middle_name: str | None
    last_name: str


@dataclass
class PatientOrm:
    id: int
    personal_info: PersonalInfoOrm


@dataclass
class DoctorOrm:
    id: int
    first_name: str
    last_name: str


# Works fine
patient_orm = PatientOrm(
    id=1,
    personal_info=PersonalInfoOrm(
        id=1,
        first_name="John",
        middle_name="Doe",
        last_name="Smith",
    ),
)
patient_get = PatientGet.model_validate(patient_orm)
sign_in = SuccessSignIn.model_validate({
    "user": patient_get,
    "user_type": "patient",
    "access_token": "access_token",
    "refresh_token": "refresh_token",
    "token_type": "bearer",
})

# Error
doctor_orm = DoctorOrm(
    id=1,
    first_name="John",
    last_name="Smith",
)
doctor_get = DoctorGet.model_validate(doctor_orm)
sign_in = SuccessSignIn.model_validate({
    "user": doctor_get,
    "user_type": "patient",

### Initial Checks

### Description

When comparing v1 vs v2 in terms the amount of details that are printed on an `AttributeError`, I very much prefer v1 and now I am wondering if it was a deliberate decision to go so verbose.

It does not add lots of value to me as a pydantic user to know in which branch of its logic the problem occured.
Knowing that the model is missing the attribute seems very fine to me.


V1 prints this:

```
def test_v1():
        class M(v1.BaseModel):
            val: int = 0
    
>       assert M().attr
E       AttributeError: 'M' object has no attribute 'attr'

test_.py:7: AttributeError
```

V2 prints this:

```
def test_v2():
        class M(BaseModel):
            val: int = 0
    
>       assert M().attr

test_.py:13: 
_ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ 

self = M(val=0), item = 'attr'

    def __getattr__(self, item: str) -> Any:
        private_attributes = object.__getattribute__(self, '__private_attributes__')
        if item in private_attributes:
            attribute = private_attributes[item]
            if hasattr(attribute, '__get__'):
                return attribute.__get__(self, type(self))  # type: ignore
    
            try:
                # Note: self.__pydantic_private__ cannot be None if self.__private_attributes__ has items
                return self.__pydantic_private__[item]  # type: ignore
            except KeyError as exc:
                raise AttributeError(f'{type(self).__name__!r} object has no attribute {item!r}') from exc

title: When using model_validator in mode=before in a child A of pydantic class, this affects also other children.
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

There is an issue with inheritance - classes of children are somehow affect one another (which I guess is not the desired behavior).
Using the code below, one can reproduce the issue:
```
import re
from typing import Optional, Union
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, model_validator

class Parent(BaseModel):
   query: str
   parameters: Optional[list] = Field(default=[])

class ChildA(Parent):
    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def extract_params_from_variables(cls, values: dict):
        print("inside model_validator A")
        values['parameters'] = re.findall("\$<([A-Z]+)>\$", str(values['query']))
        return values

class ChildB(Parent):
    variables: str

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def extract_params_from_query(cls, values: dict):
        print("inside model_validator B")
        values['parameters'] = re.findall("\$<([A-Z]+)>\$", str(values['variables']))
        return values


class TEST(BaseModel):
    child_type: str
    details: dict
    children: Optional[Union[ChildB, ChildA]] = Field(default=None)

    class Config:
        extra='allow'

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def set_children(cls, values: dict):
        if values['child_type'] == "A":
            values["children"] = ChildA(**values['details'])
        elif values['child_type'] == "B":
            values["children"] = ChildB(**values['details'])
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"unsupported value of child_type: {values['child_type']}")
        return values

if __name__=="__main__":
    # This works as expected
    c_a = ChildA(query="something somthing $<NAME>$ something")
    print("successfully worked on child A")
    c_b = ChildB(query="something somthing $<NAME>$ something", variables=" $<B>$")
    print("successfully worked on child B")

    # Here is the bug
    dicts = [
        {'child_type': 'A', 'details': {'query':"something somthing $<NAME>$ something"}},
        {'child_type': 'B', 'details': {'query': "something somthing $<NAME>$ something", 'variables':"$<B>$"}},
             ]
    for d in dicts:
        print(f"works on {d['child_type']=}")
        try:
            t = TEST(**d)
        except Exception as e:
            print(e)

    print("done")
```

Here is what I'm getting when this code runs:
```
inside model_validator A
successfully worked on child A
inside model_validator B
successfully worked on child B
works on d['child_type']='A'
inside model_validator A
inside model_validator B
'ChildA' object is not subscriptable
works on d['child_type']='B'
inside model_validator B
done
```

For some reason, when working on d['child_type']='A', the model also activates the validator of model_B. This leads to the error message: `'ChildA' object is not subscriptable` since it tried to run the validator of model B after the model_validator in model A had been running.

title: Allow for model discrimination without the creation of another BaseModel
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [X] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Hello,

I want to select the right model based on user input. The user control the value of only one field, and the rest of the model is assumed to be supplied correctly. I read about [discriminated unions](https://docs.pydantic.dev/2.0/usage/types/unions/#nested-discriminated-unions) but the slight issue is that I'm forced to create a class to be able to type one attribute of this class with the actual type union I want.

What I was imagining was a function available in pydantic that does that. Here is my implementation:

```python
def discriminate_pydantic_unions(input: dict[str, Any], model_unions: type):
    """
    This function is purely a pydantic utilitarian function. Read
    https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/9512 for more context.

    Given a union of pydantic models, will output the one that matches
    with the input. It is based on the discriminated union principle
    https://docs.pydantic.dev/2.0/usage/types/unions/#nested-discriminated-unions
    """

    class Discri(BaseModel):
        results: model_unions

    return Discri(results=input).results


class G(BaseModel):
    one: str

class H(BaseModel):
    one: int
```

It yields:

```python
discriminate_unions({"one": "h"}, G | H)
>>> G(one="h")
discriminate_unions({"one": 3}, G | H)
>>> H(one=3)
```

Here is a more elaborate example:

```python
class LikelihoodA(BaseModel):
    likelihood: Literal["a"]
    regularization: Literal["None"]

class LikelihoodB(BaseModel):
    likelihood: Literal["b"]
    regularization: Literal["None"]

class RegularizationA(BaseModel):
    regularization: Literal["a"]

class RegularizationB(BaseModel):
    regularization: Literal["b"]


linear_regression_models = Annotated[
    LikelihoodA
    | LikelihoodB,
    Field(discriminator="likelihood"),
]
regression_models = Annotated[
    RegularizationA
    | RegularizationB
    | linear_regression_models,
    Field(discriminator="regularization"),
]

discriminate_pydantic_unions({"regularization": "a"}, regression_models)
>>> RegularizationA(regularization='a')
discriminate_pydantic_unions({"regularization": "b", "likelihood": "a"}, regression_models)
>>> RegularizationB(regularization='b')
discriminate_pydantic_unions({"regularization": "None", "likelihood": "a"}, regression_models)
>>> LikelihoodA(likelihood='a')
```

### Affected Components

title: defaultdict loses its default factory in serializing/deserialising roundtrip
body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

It looks like when serializing/deserialising a `BaseModel` that holds a `defaultdict`, its `default_factory` is lost.

This has been previously reported in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/4687 for v1 and the special case of a nested defaultdict. In v2 I'm facing the issue even without nesting.

### Example Code

```py
from collections import defaultdict
from pydantic import BaseModel

class MyModel(BaseModel):
    some_dict: defaultdict[str, int] = defaultdict(lambda: 42)

instance_orig = MyModel()
print(instance_orig.some_dict["a"])  # -> 42
print(instance_orig.some_dict["b"])  # -> 42

instance_roundtrip = MyModel.model_validate_json(instance_orig.model_dump_json())
print(instance_roundtrip.some_dict["a"])  # -> 42
print(instance_roundtrip.some_dict["b"])  # -> 42
print(instance_roundtrip.some_dict["c"])  # -> 0
```

The output is:

```
42
42
42
42
0
```

Note that after the serialization/deserialization roundtrip, the specified `default_factory` is lost. This violates the invariant of the class, because it no longer behaves as intended (in this case returning 42 for missing entries).
